1. **Scene-by-scene summary of what happens**

The text opens with an editorial apparatus: Baker's Introduction situates Sidney's romance within the genealogy of English fiction, arguing that the Arcadia represents the culmination of the "middle period" between medieval romance and modern realism. Sidney's own Dedication to his sister, the Countess of Pembroke, follows, in which he dismisses the work as an "idle work" and "trifle" written for her amusement.

The narrative itself begins in Book I with two shepherds, Strephon and Claius, standing on shores opposite the island of Cythere, mourning the departure of their lady Urania. Strephon delivers an elaborate lament recalling the last time he saw her, her beauty, her speech, her farewell. Claius responds by praising Urania's virtues and the transforming power of her love, which elevated simple shepherds to intellectual pursuits.

A shipwreck survivor floats ashore—a naked young man clutching a small coffer. The shepherds revive him. He is Musidorus (later calling himself Palladius), a prince in disguise. He immediately tries to drown himself when he believes his friend Pyrocles (Daiphantus) has perished. The shepherds prevent him and learn that he seeks the body of his friend. They sail toward a burning wreck where Pyrocles was last seen. Approaching, they discover a scene of carnage—a ship destroyed, bodies floating, spoils scattered. On the mast sits a beautiful youth in his shirt, holding a sword aloft in defiant posture. The fishermen superstitiously refuse to rescue him, thinking him a god. Musidorus leaps to the mariner and throws a rope, but the ship has already passed. A pirate galley pursues them; the fishermen flee, leaving Pyrocles to be captured.

# Close Reading of "Napoleon's Letters to Josephine"

## 1. What Happens, Scene by Scene

The book opens with the title page and publishing information, followed by a preface that establishes the author's purpose: to present Napoleon's private correspondence with Josephine as essential primary source material for understanding both the man and his era. The author, Henry Foljambe Hall, argues against prevailing historiographical approaches, claiming that contemporary sources—particularly personal letters—offer more authentic insight than later historical narratives.

The introduction provides extensive scholarly apparatus, discussing the difficulties of translating Napoleon's concise French, his character as revealed through contemporaries' accounts, and the complex provenance of the letters themselves. Hall traces three main sources: the Tennant Collection (letters acquired by a Polish nobleman who served Bonaparte), the Didot Collection (228 letters published in 1833), and various fugitive letters from other sources.

Series A (1796) begins with Napoleon's appointment as Commander-in-Chief of the Army of Italy on February 23, 1796, and his marriage to Josephine on March 9. The first letter (February 23) shows Napoleon waking to think of Josephine, expressing his passion and jealousy in fevered, almost obsessive terms. Letter No. 2 (March 14) reveals his anxiety about her fidelity during his absence, oscillating between fearing she's forgotten him and worrying about her health. Letter No. 3 (April 3) from Port Maurice contains one of the most passionate declarations in the collection, where he writes that Josephine has "robbed me of more than my soul; you are the one only thought of my life."

The campaign narrative then interweaves with personal correspondence. Military actions at Montenotte, Millesimo, Dego, and Mondovi (April 10-22) are followed by letters revealing domestic tensions. Letter No. 6 (April 24) shows Napoleon urging Josephine to come to Italy, sending gifts, and expressing concern about her "wretched indigestion." Letter No. 7 (June 15) from Tortona reveals a crisis: Napoleon has received no letters and believes Josephine is ill, writing that "my life is a perpetual nightmare. A presentiment of ill oppresses me." He threatens to start for Paris immediately if her illness is dangerous.

Series B continues the pattern of intimate correspondence during active warfare. Letter No. 1 (July 6) is terse: "I have beaten the enemy... I think that I am going to be very ill." No. 2 (July 17) contains philosophical reflection on the growth of love, contradicting La Bruyère's maxim that "Love comes all at once." Grant describes his own uneventful rural childhood: attending indifferent subscription schools, working in his father's tannery and on farms, driving horses, and taking a two-hundred-mile journey to Kentucky at age fifteen where he traded horses. White's liberal use of the birch rod.

The second essay, **"On Love to One's Offspring"**, presents a philosophical argument against Epicurean views that parental affection is motivated solely by self-interest. # A Close Reading of Skeat's Edition of Chaucer's Boethius and Troilus

## 1. What Happens: The Structure of the Scholarly Apparatus

The front matter presents itself as a complete scholarly apparatus designed to contextualize two major Chaucerian texts. The Introduction to Boethius (§§ 1-27, pages vii-xlviii) moves from establishing the work's date (c. 1377-1380) through biographical information about Boethius himself, his historical circumstances under Theodoric, and the content of the Consolation of Philosophy. It traces the medieval transmission of the text through Alfred's Anglo-Saxon translation, Walton's verse rendering of 1410, and numerous continental versions. The longest sections address Chaucer's methodology as translator—his occasional inaccuracies (as when he renders Latin *clauus* as "a keye" due to confusion with *clauis*), his debt to glosses in his source manuscripts, and his extensive borrowings from Boethius throughout his later works.

The Introduction to Troilus (§§ 1-31, pages xlix-lxxxv) similarly establishes chronology (c. 1380-1382) but focuses extensively on sources. The introduction includes detailed manuscript descriptions (the Campsall MS prepared for Henry V, the Corpus Christi College MS bearing the arms of John of Gaunt's family), collation procedures, and comparisons with earlier printed editions from Caxton through Thynne.

The father has discovered that Stephen Smith—whom Elfride wishes to marry—is merely the son of Jack Smith the mason, not a gentleman of professional standing as he had believed from the architect Hewby's letter ("My assistant, Mr. Stephen Smith"). Mr. Swancourt insists that social station is fixed by birth, not profession, and forbids the match. Elfride weeps but cannot move him. Stephen insists Elfride is "too far above me." His father remains largely silent. Stephen announces he may leave for London the next day.

The narrative opens with Robert Audley, a young barrister of languid temperament, searching for his missing friend George Talboys at the Sun Inn in the village of Audley. # Close Reading of Augustine's Confessions: Books X–XI

## 1. Scene by Scene

**The text opens mid-thought**: Augustine has just described his mother Monica's death at Ostia, and now in Book X he turns inward to examine his present spiritual condition and the nature of his own soul. He cries out to God: "Let me know Thee, O Lord, who knowest me: let me know Thee, as I am known" (X.1). He frames confession not merely as accounting for past sins but as an ongoing practice of self-examination before God.

**A passage of recollection follows**: Augustine recounts his mother's final days—her illness, her peaceful death, his grief, and her burial. He emphasizes her humility and faith, and he prays for her soul. The scene at the window is the emotional center: he and Monica discuss the afterlife, and she declares she has no more desire for earthly life. Five days later she dies. Augustine weeps, then recovers, then weeps again at the memory of her "holy tenderness."

**Augustine then turns to his present life**: He describes his ongoing struggles with the "three concupiscences" (flesh, eyes, pride). He details specific temptations—food, music, visual beauty, the desire for praise—and his efforts to resist them through continence. He acknowledges that he cannot be continent without God's grace.

**Book X continues with an extensive meditation on memory**: Augustine calls memory "a great and boundless chamber" (X.8). He describes how memory works—images enter through the senses, but also abstract concepts (numbers, justice, friendship) exist in memory without images. He explores puzzles of memory: forgetting, remembering forgetfulness, and how we can discuss concepts we cannot see.

**The scene shifts to Augustine's study of Scripture**: He recalls reading Isaiah, finding it obscure, and postponing it until he knew the Gospels better. He describes his reading of Paul's letters, particularly Romans, which struck him at Milan's garden.

**In Book XI, Augustine turns to the question of time**: He asks, "What then is time?" (XI.14). He notes that we speak of long and short times, past and future, but examines how the present moment seems to have no duration. He rejects the idea that time exists without creatures moving through it. He argues that time only exists as the mind's perception of motion and change.

**The final scene presents the creation narrative**: Augustine interprets Genesis 1:1—"In the beginning Thou madest the heaven and earth." He discusses what "beginning" means, arguing that Christ is the Beginning who spoke creation into being. He addresses the philosophical puzzle of what God was doing before creation: there was no "before" without time itself.

---

## 2. Characters Who Speak or Act

**Augustine (narrator and protagonist)**: His driving concern is the desire to know God and know himself truly. He is caught between intellectual aspiration and sensual weakness. His motivation is confessional—he exposes his ongoing struggles with pride, lust of the flesh, and curiosity. He serves as both priest and penitent, offering his life as example.

**Monica (his mother)**: In the death scene, she demonstrates complete readiness for death. She tells Augustine she has no further delight in earthly life, that her hopes are fulfilled. Her motivation is faith—she has prayed for her son's conversion and now sees it accomplished. She embodies the patient, long-suffering Christian matron who has won her household for Christ through quiet example.

A major scene unfolds at the first woman's convention in Albany, where speakers including Phillips, Channing, Ernestine L. Rose, Antoinette L. Brown, and Susan B. Anthony address the legislature. The press response is hostile: Stanton quotes the *Albany Register*'s March 7, 1854 article mocking "feminine propagandists" and comparing them to circus clowns, while warning against "unsexed women" who would "step out from the true sphere of the mother, the wife, and the daughter."

The narrative shifts to the Bloomer costume experiment. Stanton describes Elizabeth Smith Miller visiting Seneca Falls in 1852 "dressed somewhat in the Turkish style—short skirt, full trousers of fine black broadcloth," finding the costume superior for mobility. Stanton adopted it for two years, experiencing "incredible freedom," though the experiment ultimately failed due to social ridicule: boys followed wearers in crowds, chanting doggerel about Bloomers.

A domestic scene in Seneca Falls shows Stanton advising a congressman's wife (Charlotte) to defy her husband and purchase a new stove without permission, coaching her on how to remain silent during his inevitable tantrum. When Mr. S. returns and discovers the stoves, Charlotte executes the strategy perfectly—he eventually accepts the new arrangement.

During the winter of 1861, Stanton, Anthony, and Beriah Green attempt anti-slavery conventions across New York State. At Buffalo's St. James' Hall, a mob organized by ex-Justice Hinson disrupts proceedings, while police make no effort to intervene. At Port Byron, opponents scatter cayenne pepper on the stove to force evacuation. Only Albany, under a Democratic mayor who "said the right of free speech should never be trodden under foot," provides protection.

A private crisis emerges behind the scenes: Anthony has helped a sane mother escape from an insane asylum where her husband had incarcerated her

# A Close Reading of the Darwin Correspondence (1859–1862)

The text presented is not a narrative but a collection of letters exchanged primarily between Charles Darwin and his scientific correspondents during the two years following the publication of *On the Origin of Species* (November 1859). What unfolds across these 135 letters is not a plotted story but an epistolary record of intellectual combat, scientific collaboration, and the slow cultural upheaval triggered by Darwin's theory. The "scenes" are the moments of composition, the dinners, the meetings, the literary exchanges; the "characters" are Darwin himself and the constellation of scientists, reviewers, and critics who responded to his work.

---

## I. Scene-by-Scene: The Correspondence as Chronicle

The letters cluster around several distinct episodes and contexts, which I will trace chronologically as the primary structure of "what happens."

**1. The Immediate Aftermath (November–December 1859)**
The book has just appeared. Darwin writes to Huxley on December 13th, arranging to send drawings of pigeon breeds and manuscript chapters on hybridism and domestic varieties. He is already planning the expanded volumes that will follow the "abstract" he has published. On December 16th, he confirms plans to attend the Philosophical Club dinner, bringing specimen skulls (Carrier and Tumbler pigeons) and manuscript. The letters reveal Darwin at this point as a man who has committed his ideas to print but is uncertain how the scientific community will receive them. He writes with characteristic self-deprecation ("I speak now in the palace of truth") and with evident anxiety about lending his only manuscript copies.

**2. The Sedgwick Letter and Early Criticism (December 1859–January 1860)**
Letter 84 references Sedgwick's "kind yet slashing" critique—Adam Sedgwick, Darwin's former professor at Cambridge, who had laughed at the book but also warned against its implications. Letter 91 sends Sedgwick's letter to Lyell, noting it is "terribly muddled, and really the first page seems almost childish." This marks one of the earliest academic rejections Darwin receives, from a man whose opinion he deeply respects. The "palace of truth" self-consciousness suggests Darwin is already steeling himself for sustained opposition.

**3. Huxley's Royal Institution Lecture (February 1860)**
Darwin attends or hears reports of Huxley's February 10th lecture at the Royal Institution defending natural selection. Letter 94 records Darwin's complicated reaction: he is grateful for the support but disappointed that Huxley "wasted time" on introductory material and failed to convey the full scope of the theory (classification, morphology, embryology). He writes: "I have always looked at the doctrine of Natural Selection as an hypothesis, which, if it explained several large classes of facts, would deserve to be ranked as a theory deserving acceptance." The lecture becomes a touchstone—Huxley is the warrior, Lyell and Hooker the allies, but Darwin himself remains the theorist who must see the whole picture.

**4. The Edinburgh Review Attack (April 1860)**
Letter 98 (to Huxley, April 9th) responds to what is now understood as Richard Owen's devastating review in the *Edinburgh Review*. Darwin catalogues the misrepresentations: a passage about "plastic minds" attributed to him that he never wrote; quotations "garbled" to change their meaning. He writes with unusual heat: "I never saw such an amount of misrepresentation" and calls the review "false and malignant." This marks the beginning of Darwin's sustained opposition to Owen, which will intensify throughout the correspondence.

The argument likens the virtuous person to a builder who uses only fine materials, contrasting such careful construction with those who heap together any chance material pell-mell.

The essay "Whether Vice Is Sufficient to Cause Unhappiness" argues that vice alone, without any external instruments, produces misery—while Fortune requires vice to cooperate fully. The argument is dramatized as a contest between personified Fortune and Vice before a hypothetical contract-builder: Fortune offers disasters (robberies, wars, storms, poison, exile), but Vice, standing naked without external apparatus, defeats her because the virtuous (Metrocles, Diogenes, Socrates, Decius) are unmoved by external calamities. Vice attacks the soul directly, filling it with sorrow, lamentation, and remorse in ways that fire and sword cannot.

"Whether the Disorders of Mind or Body Are Worse" uses a fox-and-leopard fable to claim that the mind contains internal sources of badness more dangerous than bodily diseases, because bodily illness is detected and treatable while mental disease removes the very faculty of perception. **Close reading of the opening of Jules Verne’s *The Mysterious Island***  

---

## 1. What happens – scene by scene  

1. **Discovery of the pickaxe and the cavern** – The narrator notes that the pickaxe was easily found, and a hole was seen in a line above the spot where it was stuck in the sand. Rock pigeons are already flying in and out, implying the cavern (Granite House) was intended for the castaways.  

2. **Cyrus Harding’s plan for the cavern** – Harding explains to Pencroft that the entrance should be sealed and a rope ladder used for entry, a precaution against possible intruders. Pencroft questions the need for a door; Harding replies that the natural passage could let enemies in.  

3. **Construction of windows, a door, and a rope ladder** – Using nitro‑glycerine, pickaxes, and later brick, the colonists cut five windows, a door, and a large bay window. A sturdy rope ladder (made from twisted cane fibers and red cedar rounds) is attached to a platform at 40 ft and then to the door at 80 ft. Top the dog is trained to climb it.  

4. **Dividing the interior** – The cavern is divided into five rooms (kitchen, dining‑room, sleeping‑room, “Visitor’s room”, and a storehouse). A corridor, a store‑room, and a water‑supply conduit are added, with lime‑made bricks for partitions.  

5. **Provisioning and hunting** – The colonists hunt in Jacamar Wood, discovering a natural warren full of American rabbits. Herbert gathers medicinal herbs (basil, rosemary, balm, etc.). The warren provides meat for the colony, while Spilett and Herbert capture a turtle, only to see it vanish when the tide rises.  

6. **The bullet in the peccary** – While feasting on a suckling‑pig, Pencroft cracks a tooth on a lead bullet hidden inside the meat. This reveals that a firearm has been discharged on the island within the last three months.  

7. **Construction of a bark canoe** – In five days, Pencroft builds a flat‑bottomed bark canoe, the *Pioneer*, to explore the island’s interior.

# Close Reading of Ovid, *Metamorphoses* Book VII, Fable I (Lines 1-158)

## 1. Scene-by-Scene Summary

**The Argonauts' Arrival**

The passage opens with the Minyæ (the Argonauts) having completed their voyage in the Pagasæan ship, having already visited the blind prophet Phineus and been aided by Calais and Zethes (the winged sons of Boreas). They have "reached at length the rapid waters of the muddy Phasis"—the river at the edge of the known world, in Colchis.

**Medea's Soliloquy**

The heart of the passage is an extended internal monologue in which Medea, daughter of King Æetes, struggles with her sudden, overwhelming love for the Greek stranger Jason. She debates herself at length: whether to resist love (which she terms a "new power" that "draws me on, against my will"), whether Jason deserves her aid, what she will gain by helping him (marriage, travel to Greece, glory), and what she will lose (her family, her homeland, her innocence). She ultimately decides: "By my agency thou shalt be saved; when saved, grant what thou hast promised."

**The Meeting**

Jason and Medea meet, apparently at an altar of Hecate. He takes her right hand, speaks "with a humble voice," and promises her marriage. She weeps, accepts, and gives him "some enchanted herbs" along with instruction in their use. The passage reports: "He swears by the rites of the Goddess of the triple form, and the Deity which is in that grove, and by the sire of his future father-in-law, who beholds all things."

**Jason's Trials**

The narrative moves to the actual confrontation. At dawn, the Colchian people gather on a sacred field. Æetes sits enthroned, "arrayed in purple, and distinguished by a sceptre of ivory." Jason faces three ordeals:

1. **The fire-breathing bulls**: "The brazen-footed bulls breathe forth flames from their adamantine nostrils." Jason strokes them, yokes them, and ploughs the previously untilled field.

2. **The sown dragon's teeth**: He sows the teeth of the dragon (from Cadmus's story) in the ploughed earth. They spring up as armed Earth-born men who begin fighting among themselves—Jason wins by throwing a stone to turn their violence inward.

3. **The sleeping dragon**: The final trial is to lull the guardian of the Golden Fleece. Medea's herbs ("Lethæan juice") and incantations ("words that cause placid slumbers") succeed, and Jason takes the Fleece.

**Departure**

The passage ends with Jason triumphant: "proud of the spoil and bearing with him the giver of the prize as a second spoil, he arrives victorious, with his wife, at the port of Iolcos."

---

## 2. Character Analysis

**Medea**

Medea dominates the passage through her extended interior monologue. She is defined by conflicting forces: duty to her father and country versus overwhelming passion. Her internal debate reveals a calculating mind—she catalogs what she stands to gain ("acquaintance with a better country, and cities, whose fame is flourishing even here"), what she stands to lose ("my father is cruel... my country, too, is barbarous"), and what moral weight she must bear ("Do but consider how great an offence thou art meditating").

Her agency is striking: she is not a passive object but an active agent who decides to betray her kingdom. The text makes clear she understands this as criminal ("thy criminality") but chooses it anyway. **1. What happens, scene by scene**

The text opens not with narrative but with an elaborate apology. Coleridge defends himself against anticipated objections to his literary biography. He introduces the phrase “Tetrachordon,” alludes to his translation of Psalms, and argues that dwelling too long on poetic beauties would mislead future writers into imitating a poet’s anomalies rather than his excellences. He attacks contemporary reviewers for lacking fixed critical canons, for arbitrary dictation, and for preferring fault-finding over the elucidation of beauty. He then moves into an extended eulogy of Robert Southey, cataloguing his versatility as poet, historian, essayist, and moral man, defending him against anonymous critics and insisting that Southey’s character—his industry, domestic virtues, and moral purity—justifies public testimony in his favour.

The tone shifts in Chapter IV to the Lyrical Ballads. Coleridge argues that Wordsworth’s two volumes of Lyrical Ballads were not the true cause of the controversy surrounding the "Lake School." Rather, he contends, Wordsworth’s own preface and critical remarks generated the opposition. He analyses the reaction of readers, noting that different critics objected to entirely different poems, suggesting the hostility was disproportionate to the poems’ faults. He introduces his own first encounter with Wordsworth’s Descriptive Sketches (1794), praising its emergent genius but noting its harshness and obscurity, and describes a later manuscript recitation by Wordsworth that impressed him profoundly with its union of deep feeling and original imagination.

From personal memoir Coleridge pivots to philosophy. He announces his central thesis: that Fancy and Imagination are two distinct faculties, not synonyms or degrees of one power. He traces the history of associationism from Aristotle through Vives, Descartes, Hobbes, and Hartley, arguing that Hartley’s mechanical vibration theory is untenable because it cannot explain how different causes produce associated ideas. He offers an extended anecdote about a young German woman possessed by a “learned devil” during fever, which he uses to argue that all thoughts are in themselves imperishable—a prelude to theological speculation he defers “for a loftier mood.” Chapter VII exposes the consequences of Hartley's theory: if association alone governs mind, the will and reason become its creatures, and human agency is illusory. He introduces an insect on a stream as emblematic of the mind’s alternating active and passive movements, and locates the intermediate faculty in the Imagination.

Chapter VIII surveys dualism, hylozoism, and materialism, concluding each is inadequate to explain perception. Chapter IX is autobiographical and intellectual: Coleridge describes his philosophical wanderings through Locke, Berkeley, Leibniz, and Hartley, his debt to the mystics (Boehme, Tauler, Fox, William Law), and his formative encounter with Kant, whose critical philosophy he describes as taking possession of him “as with the giant’s hand.” He discusses Kant’s caution, Fichte’s overbuilt egoism, and his own obligations to Schelling, asserting that coincidences of thought between them arise from shared philosophical precursors, not borrowing. The text comprises three distinct treatises from Plutarch's *Moralia*, progressing through interconnected discussions of social virtue.

Section XVI shows flatterers declaring the rich man "at once orator and poet, and (if he likes) painter, and flute-player"—a grotesque inflation that reveals its own absurdity. Section XVII introduces false *parrhesia*: the flatterer's "outspokenness" attacks trifles (a pot out of place, bad attire) while ignoring genuine crimes—"just as if the trainer in a gymnasium were to allow the athlete to get drunk and live in debauchery, and yet be vexed at the condition of his oil-flask." Section XVIII offers two exempla: Agis the Argive who criticized Alexander's rewards to buffoons, and a senator who prefaced supposed criticism of Tiberius with flattery disguised as boldness—ending with Cassius Severus's verdict: "This outspokenness will ruin the man."

Section XX presents the diagnostic test: "purposely giving strange advice and suggestions, and by adopting absurd corrections"—if the flatterer "nods assent to everything," he reveals himself. Section XXII contrasts the friend's promise ("If I can do it, and 'tis to be done") with the flatterer's ("Speak out your mind, whate'er it is, to me"). The friend benefits "imperceptibly," like Arcesilaus who left twenty drachmae under Apelles' pillow; the flatterer "not only reminds us of his services afterwards, but even during the very moment of doing them upbraids us with them."

# Close Reading of Mark Twain's *A Connecticut Yankee in King Arthur's Court* (Selected Passages)

## 1. What Happens, Scene by Scene

The passage encompasses a massive sweep of the novel, moving through distinct phases:

**The Money and the Feast.** The narrative opens with the introduction of a decimal currency system—dollars, cents, mills, and milrays—whose adoption the Yankee narrator regards as proof of progress. He befriends the blacksmith Dowley, a prosperous master craftsman, and invites him along with other craftsmen (the mason Dickon, the wheelwright Smug) to dine at the home of his host Marco. The Yankee secretly pays for the entire elaborate meal, which includes fresh meat, white bread, beer, and new furniture, so that Marco will not be bankrupted. The feast becomes an occasion for the Yankee to display his wealth and challenge Dowley's boasting about his own prosperity.

**The Economic Debate.** At the dinner, Dowley extols the "protection" system of his kingdom, claiming higher wages than the Yankee's country. The Yankee methodically dismantles this claim by comparing prices: salt costs twice as much, eggs more, beer more, wheat more, clothing more. He argues that "high wages" mean nothing without purchasing power—that a dollar in one country buys less than a dollar in another. Dowley fails to grasp the argument. The Yankee then invokes an "unwritten law" of wages, predicting future wage levels centuries hence and describing how workers will eventually organize to demand better conditions. He catches Dowley in a legal trap: Dowley had boasted of paying workers above the legally fixed maximum, an offense punishable by the pillory. The Yankee threatens to report him, terrifying the assembled craftsmen.

**The King's Blunder and the Mob.** The disguised King Arthur, passing as a simple farmer named Jones, launches into an incomprehensible monologue about agriculture—onions, plums, goats—which terrifies the guests, who interpret it as madness or heresy. The craftsmen attack; a fight ensues in which Arthur and the Yankee subdue them. They flee with the peasants in pursuit, hide in a tree, but are eventually smoked out and captured by the mob.

**The Slave Market.** A nobleman named Earl Grip rescues them, but then sells them as slaves at auction. Arthur brings only seven dollars; the Yankee, nine. # A Close Reading of *Pride and Prejudice*, Chapters XLVIII–LVIII

## 1. What Happens, Scene by Scene

**The journey home.** Elizabeth and the Gardiners travel from Gracechurch Street back to Longbourn as expeditiously as possible, sleeping one night on the road. Elizabeth is consumed by self-reproach. They arrive by dinnertime.

**The reunion at Longbourn.** The Gardiners' children greet them joyfully. Jane runs downstairs and meets Elizabeth in the vestibule. Elizabeth asks about news of Lydia; Jane has received only a brief letter from Mr. Bennet saying he arrived safely but will not write again until he has something important. Jane's spirits are pale. They go to see Mrs. Bennet, who receives them with tears, lamentations, and blame of everyone but herself—particularly the Forsters. Mr. Gardiner promises to go to London the next day to assist Mr. Bennet. Mary offers moral consolation that Elizabeth finds infuriating. Mrs. Bennet is eventually left alone with the housekeeper, who is the only servant deemed discreet enough to hear her.

**Elizabeth and Jane confer privately.** Jane relates details: Colonel Forster suspected partiality between Lydia and Wickham but had no alarm. Denny denied knowing of the elopement plan. Kitty had known from Lydia's last letter that the two were in love. Jane reads Lydia's note to Harriet Forster—the giddy, joking letter announcing the plan to go to Gretna Green and sign her name Lydia Wickham. Elizabeth reads it and cries, "Oh, thoughtless, thoughtless Lydia!" Jane describes how Mr. Bennet was stunned into silence for ten minutes.

**Mr. Bennet returns from London, unsuccessful.** He has pursued leads at Epsom and Clapham and intends to inquire at London's hotels. He arrives looking composed. At tea he speaks of his blame: "It has been my own doing, and I ought to feel it." He resolves to keep officers away from his house and to be far more cautious with Kitty.

**The Gardiners leave.** Mrs. Gardiner departs with the children; she has been puzzled by Elizabeth's low spirits, suspecting some connection to her "Derbyshire friend"—Mr. Darcy—whose name Elizabeth has never voluntarily mentioned. Mr. Gardiner remains in London with Mr. Bennet.

**A letter from Mr. Collins arrives.** He writes to condole with Mr. Bennet on Lydia's disgrace, assures them the fault lies in parental indulgence and a naturally bad disposition, and warns that this will injure the fortunes of the other daughters. Lady Catherine and Miss de Bourgh, to whom Collins has related the affair, share his apprehensions.

**Mr. Gardiner's letter arrives by express.** He has found Lydia and Wickham in London. They are not married and have no intention of marrying—unless terms can be settled. Gardiner has undertaken to secure Lydia's virtue by forcing a marriage. The terms: a settlement on Lydia of her equal share of the five thousand pounds and one hundred pounds per annum during Mr. Bennet's life. This, Gardiner writes, will settle on his niece "in addition to her own fortune," and Wickham's debts (over a thousand pounds) will be cleared. The marriage will take place from Gardiner's house. Mr. Gardiner asks Mr. Bennet for full powers to act in his name.

**The family reacts.** Mr. Bennet observes that Wickham is a fool to marry on so little; he would have expected ten thousand pounds. He writes his approval and sends full powers. Mrs. Bennet explodes with joy—wedding clothes, carriages, her daughter married at sixteen. ## 1. What Happens, Scene by Scene

The passage opens with the group—Dr. Seward, Van Helsing, Lord Godalming, Quincey Morris, and Jonathan Harker—convening to plan their campaign against Count Dracula. Van Helsing outlines their strategy: to trace the fifty boxes of earth that were transported from Transylvania to Carfax, and to either capture or destroy the Count, or "sterilise the earth" so he can no longer seek refuge in it. The scene is interrupted by a pistol shot—Morris has fired at a bat that frightened him, shattering the window glass. This incident, seemingly trivial, establishes the pervasive atmosphere of dread and the men's heightened sensitivity to any threat.

The men depart for Carfax to investigate, leaving Mina Harker behind at Dr. Seward's asylum. She resists being excluded but ultimately acquiesces to their chivalric protection. Seward's diary then records an urgent summons from Renfield, his zoophagous (life-consuming) patient, who demands immediate release. Van Helsing accompanies Seward to interview Renfield, and the lunatic displays unexpected eloquence and rationality, referencing his acquaintance with Lord Godalming's father and demonstrating knowledge of world affairs that puzzles his observers. When his request is denied, Renfield falls into desperate supplication, pleading to be released "for the sake of others," hinting at a purpose he cannot disclose. He speaks of his fear of being "burdened with souls" and his desire for "life," confessing that he has "friends—good friends—like you, Dr. Seward." The scene ends with Renfield's collapse into sullen acquiescence when he perceives his appeal has failed.

The next day, Jonathan Harker pursues the trail of the missing earth-boxes. He locates Thomas Snelling and Joseph Smollet, the carters who transported boxes from Carfax. Smollet provides crucial intelligence: six boxes were delivered to 197 Chicksand Street, Mile End New Town, and another six to Jamaica Lane, Bermondsey. Harker then tracks down Sam Bloxam, who reveals that he transported nine boxes from a house in Piccadilly—near a "big white church"—to Carfax. The Count himself helped load the boxes, described as "the strongest chap I ever struck," with "a white moustache." Harker locates the Piccadilly house: a deserted, dusty mansion with a stone front and high steps. He cannot ascertain the owner through Mitchell, Sons & Candy, who invoke client confidentiality until Harker invokes Lord Godalming's name, prompting the agents to promise information by post.

At the asylum, Van Helsing interviews Renfield again. The patient is sullen and refuses to speak, cursing Van Helsing as an "old fool." The passage opens in the final movements of a Mardi-Gras celebration in New Orleans, with the narrator and his party having toured the old French/Spanish Quarter under the guidance of George Washington Cable, the author of *The Grandissimes*. They visit the old St. Louis Hotel (now municipal offices), the Cathedral, and the square in front of it. They drive beyond the city into the surrounding swamp along a shell road, past cypresses, alligators, and colored figures fishing, arriving at West End on Lake Pontchartrain, where they dine on pompano. On subsequent days they attend an editorial dinner featuring Louisiana seafood (crayfish, soft-shell crabs, deviled whitebait), and witness the "Broom Brigade"—young women drilling with brooms in military formation. Inside the Washington Artillery building they see Civil War relics and a painting of Stonewall Jackson and Robert E. Lee, which Twain analyzes as a picture whose meaning is entirely dependent on its label.

The narrative then shifts to a sustained examination of Southern speech, dialect, and manners. Twain catalogs the disappearance of the consonant *r* in educated Southern speech, the insertion of *y* before *k* sounds, the frequent use of "Sir," and the "infelicities" of Southern grammar—such as "like" for "as" and the redundant "at" in "Where have you been at?" He introduces the word *lagniappe*—something thrown in for free—and demonstrates its uses in shopping, drinking, compliment-making, and restaurant service.

Chapter 45 opens with an extended meditation on why the Civil War dominates Southern conversation in a way it no longer does in the North. A club anecdote follows: a poet tries to discuss the moon but is interrupted by a war story within minutes, confirming the observation. The narrator then attends a cockfight, a mule race, and reflects on the nature of Southern reporting. He contrasts the spare, direct style of the New Orleans newspaper editor with the overwritten, "Walter Scott" prose of the average Southern correspondent, quoting examples that overembellish mundane events (ladies boarding a steamer, a mule race) with phrases like "the beauty and the chivalry of New Orleans."

Chapter 46 is a sweeping cultural critique. Twain argues that Sir Walter Scott "did measureless harm" to the South by implanting a romantic, medieval worldview—a "sham chivalry"—that delayed the region's modernization. He traces Southern character traits (dueling, inflated speech, caste reverence) directly to Scott's influence, claims Scott's fiction was partly responsible for the Civil War, and argues that Southern literature remains crippled because it clings to an obsolete romantic style while the North has moved on. Chapter 48 centers on a visit to ex-Governor Warmouth's sugar plantation, reached by tug through the swamp. On the return tug, a parrot heckles sentimental singing. The conversation among steamboatmen reveals that four out of five former river pilots who left the river became farmers—a retreat that never quite succeeds, since they must return each winter to pay off farm debts. The following morning, he reveals his impending death to Emily. He extracts two solemn vows from her: to burn certain papers hidden in a closet at La Vallée without reading them, and never to sell the château. After receiving last rites from a monk, St. Aubert dies in the afternoon with Emily present. The funeral takes place at the convent of St. Clair, where he's buried near the Villeroi family tomb.

Madame Cheron, Emily's aunt, represents vanity, worldliness, and a desire for control. She seeks to assert authority over her niece and insists on taking her to Thoulouse.

## Close Reading

### 1. What Happens, Scene by Scene

The opening section frames a biographical narrative through the Renaissance geographer Giovanni Battista Ramusio, who in 1553 composed the first sustained account of Marco Polo's life. Ramusio's preface moves through several distinct scenes: first, he establishes Polo's significance by comparing him to Ptolemy and Columbus, arguing that Polo's overland journey to Cathay was more arduous than Columbus's sea voyage. Second, he narrates the dramatic return of the three Polo travelers—Nicolo, Maffeo, and young Marco—to Venice after twenty-six years abroad, describing how their own relatives failed to recognize them. Third, the scene shifts to a banquet where the Polos prove their identity by cutting open their ragged traveling clothes to reveal jewels sewn into the linings. Fourth, Ramusio recounts Marco's subsequent capture at the Battle of Curzola in 1298, where his galley pressed forward too eagerly, was cut off, and he was taken prisoner by the Genoese. Fifth, in Genoese captivity, Marco dictated his book to a fellow prisoner, Rusticiano of Pisa, initially in Latin. Finally, Ramusio traces the family genealogy forward to 1417, when the last male Polo died childless.

### 2. Characters and Their Drives

**Ramusio** functions as both editor and advocate. His drive is scholarly and nationalistic—he wishes to vindicate Polo's geographical accuracy against centuries of dismissal as a "fabulist" and to establish Venetian primacy in exploration. His tone reveals a combative energy: "It makes one marvel to consider the immense extent of the journeys made," he writes, then pivots to defensiveness about European skepticism.

**Marco Polo** emerges through Ramusio's account as a figure defined by displacement and performance. His fundamental drive, as rendered here, is recognition—both literal (the relatives who do not know him) and figurative (the historical reputation his book must earn). His character combines naivety with practical cunning; he rises from bewildered youth to a "wise and discreet man" capable of managing complex social situations.

**Nicolo and Maffeo Polo** are rendered more sketchily. They function as mentors and companions to Marco, but their individual drives remain subordinated to the collective narrative of family return. **Close Reading of the Chronicle**

The text opens with a valedictory gesture—"Adieu, dear, I embrace you. NAPOLEON"—immediately establishing the epistolary form that will structure the entire work. What follows is not a continuous narrative but rather a chronicle interweaving dated historical events with Napoleon's letters to Josephine during his military campaigns from October 1805 through at least 1812.

**I. Scene-by-Scene Progression**

The chronicle proceeds through distinct campaign periods. The 1805 Austrian campaign opens with the Battle of Hasslach (October 11th), followed by the French entry into Munich (October 12th), and culminates in the capitulation of Ulm (October 17th). Napoleon's letters during this period are brief battlefield communications—announcing victories, assuring Josephine of his health, and expressing affection despite terrible weather conditions. The tone shifts following the Battle of Austerlitz (December 2, 1805), where Napoleon writes exultantly of a decisive victory, then documents the subsequent diplomatic negotiations culminating in the Peace of Pressburg (December 27th).

The Prussian campaign of 1806 opens with the declaration of war (October 8th) and progresses through the victories at Jena and Auerstadt (October 14th), the capture of Berlin (October 25th), and the pursuit into Poland. Napoleon's letters become longer, more reflective, and increasingly solicitous about Josephine's emotional state. He writes from Berlin (November 1806) detailing his military successes while also addressing her tears and unhappiness. The Polish winter campaign brings a marked tonal change—letters describe wretched barns, mud, and rain (December 29, 1806), yet maintain assurances of affection.

The 1807 campaign through Eylau and Friedland shows Napoleon writing from field positions, documenting casualties, and expressing both military confidence and personal fatigue. The Tilsit negotiations (June-July 1807) introduce Alexander of Russia as a recurring presence in the correspondence, with Napoleon describing the Tsar's charm and his own diplomatic success.

A brief Italian journey (November-December 1807) yields only three letters, while the Bayonne correspondence (April 1808) documents Spanish political machinations and the birth of Hortense's son (Charles Louis Napoleon, future Napoleon III). The creature reappears at night, its electric light visible for miles; the frigate pursues it at increasing speeds, reaching 18½ miles per hour, but the narwhal matches the ship exactly, "swimming too at the rate of 18½ miles an hour." A gunshot wounds it but does not kill it—the bullet "sliding off the rounded surface" of its armor. As night falls, the creature appears again, seemingly sleeping on the surface. Ned Land, the harpooner, positions himself to strike, but the moment his harpoon connects, "two enormous waterspouts broke over the bridge of the frigate," and the narrator is thrown into the sea.

Aronnax struggles in darkness, his clothes weighing him down, until Conseil—his faithful servant—appears and cuts away his garments. The two swim together, taking turns supporting each other, for hours through phosphorescent waters. Just as Aronnax sinks, he is pulled onto "a hard body"—the back of the narwhal, which is revealed to be "a sort of submarine boat," made of "sheet iron." Ned Land joins them on the vessel's surface. The three are dragged inside by masked men.

Inside the vessel, they find themselves prisoners in a sealed cabin that floods with electric light. After attempts at communication in French, English, German, and Latin fail, a steward brings food bearing the motto "MOBILIS IN MOBILI N"—the ship's name and the initial of its commander. They sleep, and wake to discover fresh air has been pumped in, confirming the vessel surfaces to breathe like a whale. A steward's arrival triggers Ned Land's violence, but before he can harm the man, the commander himself appears, speaking perfect French. He explains that Aronnax and his companions will remain as prisoners but will be treated with hospitality; in exchange, they must submit to occasional confinement and give their "word of honour" never to attempt escape. Ned refuses. Aronnax accepts conditionally.

Captain Nemo—his name is now revealed—shows Aronnax the *Nautilus*: its library, drawing-room filled with art and scientific specimens, dining room where the food is entirely marine in origin. He explains the ship's electrical power, derived from sodium extracted from seawater. The *Nautilus* is 232 feet long, displaces 1,500 tons, and can travel at fifty miles per hour. Nemo demonstrates steering with inclined planes that allow diagonal ascent or descent, and a screw that can propel the vessel vertically like a balloon.

The excerpt opens with Colonel Jeffery and an unnamed friend (later identified as a captain) standing near Sweeney Todd's shop in Fleet Street. Jeffery wants to enter the barbershop alone to investigate his suspicions about Todd, but his companion insists this would be reckless. They agree to seek official help and proceed to Sir Richard Blunt, a magistrate. Blunt expresses interest in the case and reveals he has long suspected Todd of criminal conduct after a previous incident involving stolen shoe-buckles. He dispatches a rough subordinate named Crotchet to observe Todd's shop while he himself visits St. Dunstan's church, where a foul stench has been reported—a detail that subtly connects to the novel's central horror.

Simultaneously, the narrative shifts to Tobias Ragg, a boy whom Todd has had committed to Mr. Fogg's private madhouse at Peckham Rye. Tobias lies in a dungeon-like cell, initially in a stupor. He becomes aware of a female voice singing nearby—sweet but occasionally wild, leading him to suspect his fellow inmate is mad. When Tobias cries out for help, the singer shrieks, and a keeper enters, whipping the woman into silence. Tobias is brought before Mr. Fogg and a visiting physician, Dr. Popplejoy, an elderly, half-blind doctor bribed to approve whatever Fogg wishes. Fogg labels Tobias a monomaniac obsessed with the false idea that Sweeney Todd is a murderer. Tobias protests his sanity and is removed. Enraged by this injustice, Tobias attacks the keeper Watson, scratching his face badly.

Tobias discovers his cell door has been left unlocked in Watson's anger. He creeps into a passage and overhears Fogg and Watson plotting to murder him that night by starvation or worse. He retreats to another cell, where he finds the woman who had been singing. She is not mad but a long-term inmate who has befriended Tobias. She reveals she was imprisoned by her own parents, who wanted her dead so they could inherit her inheritance from a deceased aunt. She has dug a tunnel under the cell floor leading to a woodshed in the garden. They plan to escape at night using a rope made from a torn quilt.

They begin their escape: Tobias climbs a tree to the garden wall and lowers the rope. The woman climbs, but the rope breaks, and she falls. Alarms are raised. Tobias drops to the ground, injures himself, and flees. The woman is recaptured. Tobias runs through the Surrey roads toward London, pursued by people who think him mad, until he collapses on London Bridge. Colonel Jeffery, coincidentally present, recognizes him and has him carried to a surgeon. Tobias is in a state of collapse and severe mental agitation.

At Jeffery's house, Tobias wakes in violent paroxysms, raving about Todd, his dead father, and blood. The surgeon Mr. Chisolm administers an opiate. Sir Richard Blunt promises to bring Tobias's mother, Mrs. Ragg, to help recover him.

# A Close Reading of Florence Nightingale's Later Years (1869–1879)

## 1. What Happens, Scene by Scene

The text opens with a letter dated April 22, 1869, addressed to a "Discontented Nurse." Florence Nightingale defends her own patient submission to authority—recounting how she was shut out of hospitals, refused rations for her nurses—yet remained friends with officials afterward. She explains this forbearance as service to her "Master's work," insisting that offenses against her are offenses against God, and that she must bear what her Master chooses to bear. This establishes her spiritual framework immediately: obedience as sanctity, suffering as ministry.

The scene shifts to 1867–1871, focusing on a failure at King's College Hospital's Midwifery School, which closed due to high mortality in lying-in wards. Nightingale investigates statistics on childbed mortality nationally and internationally, finding that institutional death rates far exceeded home delivery rates. She publishes *Introductory Notes on Lying-in Institutions* in October 1871, advocating for sanitary standards, training schools for midwives, and "Midwifery as a Career for Educated Women." A notable detail: Dr. Sutherland sends proofs with the warning that "dear sisters" (women's rights advocates) may "break your windows" with opposition, yet the facts are too strong to suppress.

The Franco-Prussian War (1870–1871) interrupts her work. A detailed scene describes her behind-the-scenes involvement with the National Society for Aid to the Sick and Wounded (later the British Red Cross). Letters reveal her correspondence with the Crown Princess of Prussia, her criticism of Prussian hospital conditions ("abnormally bad among the Crimean hospitals were luxurious compared with the normal Prussian hospitals"), and her plea for clemency toward France. She collects money and supplies obsessively, writing to Harriet Martineau about the "rush of all English-speaking people" contributing "every penny they could so ill spare." The text includes a vivid anecdote about Madame Werckner of Breslau, who nightly tended frozen French prisoners arriving in open trucks.

By 1872, Nightingale declares "This year I go out of office." Her official influence has waned since Gladstone's government, and she withdraws from War Office connections. Mr. Jowett urges her toward literary work—"The way of influencing mankind by ideas is the more excellent way." She begins publishing essays in *Fraser's Magazine* (May and July 1873): "A 'Note' of Interrogation" and "A Sub-Note of Interrogation: What will our Religion be in 1999." A third paper on "social reform" and "Moral Budget" is drafted but not published; Carlyle criticizes the second as "a lost lamb bleating on the mountain."

Her father dies in January 1874—she learns of it while in London, missing the funeral. She goes to Embley to manage affairs. Her mother's financial situation, servants, property questions overwhelm her. She writes: "What makes the difference between man and woman? Quetelet did his work, and I am so disturbed by my family that I can't do mine." Mrs. Bracebridge dies eighteen days later. Nightingale calls her "more than mother to me."

Parallel to external events, the text details her mystical devotions. She collects and translates passages from Catholic mystics (St. Teresa, Thomas à Kempis, St. John of the Cross) with the intention of publishing *Notes from Devotional Authors of the Middle Ages*, though the project remains unfinished. Her private meditations—written at night during sleeplessness—reveal intense self-abasement: "Am I she who once stood on that Crimean height? 'The Lady with a Lamp shall stand.' The lamp shows me only my utter shipwreck." Yet she finds strength in "the Way of the Cross," submitting her will to divine providence.

The final substantial section covers her nursing school at St. Thomas's (1872–1879). She institutes reforms: stricter selection of probationers, better instruction, a Home Sister for moral training, and regular examinations. # A Close Reading of Plutarch's "On Love," "Conjugal Precepts," and "Consolatory Letter to His Wife"

---

## 1. What Happens, Scene by Scene

### Section II–V: The Discourse on Natural Affection

The text opens with a philosophical argument establishing that animals demonstrate disinterested love for their offspring, unlike humans whom the author (through the voice of a philosopher figure) accuses of mercenary motives in procreation. The speaker describes how animals—kingfishers, cats, bears, lions, birds, partridges, and hens—all exhibit remarkable care, sacrifice, and protective instincts toward their young without expectation of return. This zoological survey serves as counter-evidence against Epicurus and those who claim that "Man loves man only for reward." The argument establishes nature's implanted affection as the true foundation of parental love.

### The Dialogue "On Love" (Sections I–XXVI)

The scene shifts to Mount Helicon during a festival to the God of Love held by the people of Thespiae. **Flavianus** and **Autobulus** (brothers, sons of the narrator's father) open the dialogue, with Autobulus about to narrate conversations that occurred "among the Muses."

The central plot concerns **Ismenodora**, "a lady called Ismenodora, famous for her wealth and good family, and of uncommon good repute for her virtuous life," who falls in love with **Baccho**, "the son of a friend and crony of hers." Ismenodora seeks to marry Baccho despite his youth, sparking dispute among his friends and lovers.

**Pisias** and **Anthemion** (both "men of good repute, and very great friends of Baccho") are selected as arbiters. Pisias objects to the marriage on grounds of Baccho's youth and Ismenodora's wealth: "let every woman have a lover; but we ought to guard against giving the wealth of Ismenodora to Baccho, lest, if we involve him in so much grandeur and magnificence, we unwittingly lose him in it." Anthemion favors the match, arguing that Baccho needs guidance and Ismenodora can provide it: "a sensible woman rather older than her husband would direct well the life of a young man."

**Protogenes** and **Daphnaeus** join the debate. Protogenes argues that genuine love (specifically pederastic love) aims at virtue and friendship, while heterosexual love merely pursues "carnal enjoyment." Daphnaeus counters that the love of women is natural and leads to friendship after "the favor," while male-male love is "altogether a foul and unlovely favour."

The narrator's father intervenes: "I interposed, and took Protogenes by the hand." He defends conjugal love by attacking wealth-based objections and praising Ismenodora's virtue: "To select a wife for wealth rather than for her excellence or family is dishonourable and illiberal; but it is silly to reject wealth when it is accompanied by excellence and family."

In Section X, Ismenodora takes decisive action: "she sent for the most active and intimate of her male friends, and for some of her female cronies, and instructed them as to what part they should play, and waited for the hour when Baccho was accustomed regularly to pass by her house on his way to the wrestling-school." She seizes Baccho, dresses him in bridal robes, and announces the marriage. The townspeople react with laughter and indignation; the superintendents of the gymnasium debate intervention.

Pisias departs in outrage: "Ye gods, what will be the end of license like this which will overthrow our town?" But **Soclarus** suggests a counter-interpretation: perhaps Baccho orchestrated the seizure to escape his male lovers' "clutches."

# A Close Reading of Chaucer's Boethius, Book I

## 1. What Happens, Scene by Scene

The text opens with Boethius lamenting his fall from grace in **Metre I**, where he bewails his exile and the betrayal of Fortune. He weeps,addressing the Muses, whom he calls his former companions in scholarly delight but now witnesses to his wretched state. The poem describes how old age has come upon him prematurely through sorrow, and how his once-favored life has been overturned by Fortune's changeable wheel. The Muses weep with him, and he addresses friends who once congratulated his prosperity, asking why they boasted when "he that hath fallen stood nat in stedefast degree" (line 22).

In **Prose I**, Boethius sits weeping and considering his fate when a woman of imperial authority appears above his head. She is of indeterminate height—sometimes shrinking to ordinary human size, sometimes reaching heaven with her head. Her robes are woven with subtle threads and show Greek letters: a **P** (practical life) and a **T** (contemplative life), with ladder-like degrees between them, though some have torn the cloth and stolen pieces. She carries books in her right hand and a sceptre in her left. When she sees the poetic Muses surrounding Boethius's bed, she is angry, calling them "commune strompetes" (common prostitutes) of the theatre who feed his sorrows with "swete venim" (sweet poison) rather than curing them. She banishes them, declaring herself the true physician who will heal him. After the Muses depart in shame, Boethius, unable to see clearly through tears, asks who this woman is.

**Metre II** continues the allegory, describing how humans immersed in worldly troubles forget their true nature and wander into "foreine derknesses" (alien darknesses), driven by "worldly windes." The man who once beheld the heavens, studied astronomy, and investigated natural causes now lies with his neck pressed by heavy chains, forced to look down at the foolish earth.

**Prose II** has Philosophy draw near and place her hand on Boethius's chest, saying "Here nis no peril" (Here is no danger). She reminds him she nursed him with her milk and gave him armor that would have defended him had he not cast it away. She asks if he has forgotten her, and when he remains silent, she wipe his eyes with the fold of her garment, clearing away the tears.

**Metre III** describes the effect: night is chased away, darkness flees, and Boethius's eyes recover their strength—similarly to how the sun emerges after clouds and storms are dispersed by the north wind Boreas.

# A Close Reading of *Middlemarch* Chapters XII–XVII

The text opens in medias res, within the Vincy household, where Mrs. Vincy and her son Fred discuss old Mr. Featherstone's declining health, the inheritance expectations surrounding him, and the family's anxiety about Fred's prospects. This conversation establishes the central tension of the opening: Fred's financial irresponsibility and the family's hope that he will inherit from his uncle. Mrs. Vincy dismisses Mary Garth as unsuitable—"a dreadful plain girl—more fit for a governess"—while Fred defends her, revealing his attachment. The scene establishes the material and romantic preoccupations that will drive the narrative's early movements.

The scene shifts to the next morning, as Fred and his sister Rosamond ride toward Stone Court. The journey provides Eliot with an opportunity for extended pastoral description, but this landscape is not merely decorative: it encodes social reality. Lowick is "not a parish of muddy lanes and poor tenants," and Stone Court itself is visible from a distance, its farm-buildings marking it as the substantial dwelling of "a gentleman farmer." Upon arriving, they see Mrs. Waule's yellow gig—described as "more funereal than a hearse"—which signals the intrusion of the Featherstone relations into what Fred and Rosamond had hoped would be a private visit. The competition for Featherstone's favor is already underway, and the Waules are among its contestants.

Inside Stone Court, Mrs. Waule has arrived before them and is engaged in conversation with Mr. Featherstone. The dialogue reveals the specific nature of the family dispute: Mrs. Waule has heard reports—apparently originating from Mr. Bulstrode—that Fred Vincy has been "raising money on his expectations," borrowing against the anticipated inheritance. Featherstone dismisses this but demands documentation. Mrs. Waule's speech is rendered in a distinctive monotone: "a low, muffled, neutral tone, as of a voice heard through cotton wool." Her face is described as "neutral as her voice; having mere chinks for eyes, and lips that hardly moved in speaking." This physical description conveys her emotional restraint, which cracks only when she speaks of her brother's mortality: "people who are no more Featherstones than the Merry-Andrew at the fair, openly reckoning on your property coming to _them_." The scene establishes that Featherstone has no children from either marriage and that the distribution of his estate is a matter of urgent interest to multiple parties.

# Close Reading of "Life on the Mississippi" (Excerpts)

## 1. What Happens, Scene by Scene

The text opens in the midst of an already-established conflict: a captain arrives to hire steamboat pilots, but discovers that the local pilots' association will not work with a non-association pilot named S----. The association's secretary demands that the captain discharge S---- and accept an association pilot instead, forcing the captain to pay S---- approximately one thousand dollars in severance. This incident marks the beginning of the association's aggressive expansion, as non-association pilots are systematically driven out of work until they capitulate and pay substantial initiation fees to join. The association then controls pilot licensing entirely through its monopoly on the river's information network—reports deposited in locked boxes at wharf-boats, shared only among members, give association pilots decisive advantages over outsiders who must navigate with outdated information.

The narrative then shifts to describe the mechanics of steamboat racing, which the text presents as both glorious spectacle and precisely regulated competition. Boats are stripped of weight, loaded to exact drafts, and crewed with double shifts to maximize speed. The narrative documents specific record times between New Orleans and Cairo, calculating that the celebrated R. E. Lee's "fastest trip" actually represented a slower average speed than earlier voyages because the river had shortened through cut-offs. The text includes a characteristic comic interpolation about the narrator's own notoriously slow boat, the John J. Roe.

A substantial section introduces Stephen, a character defined entirely by his perpetual indebtedness and theatrical remorse. Stephen borrows money from pilots and captains, never repays, but constantly haunts his creditors with elaborate apologies and promises. His climax comes when he announces to a crowd of creditors that he has found a method to pay all debts—then reveals he will pay them "in alphabetical order," meaning those whose names begin with early letters will never see repayment before the speaker dies.

The autobiographical core follows: the narrator, as a young apprentice cub, serves under the tyrannical pilot Brown. Brown's behavior is systematically abusive—he criticizes every action, invents faults where none exist, and berates the narrator with inventive profanity. The narrator's resentment manifests in nightly fantasies of killing Brown. The conflict escalates when the narrator defends a young deckhand named Henry against Brown's false accusation, strikes Brown with a stool, and nearly comes to blows. The captain, upon hearing the matter privately, expresses disapproval of the assault but tells the narrator to "lay for him ashore" and thrash Brown later.

The narrative reaches its catastrophe when the Pennsylvania steamboat explodes near Ship Island, killing approximately one hundred fifty people. The explosion occurs while George Ealer pilots alone, with most crew asleep; the forward third of the boat is destroyed. Among the dead are Brown and the chief clerk; Henry, the narrator's brother, survives the initial explosion but drowns after swimming back to help. The narrator arrives in Memphis to find the wounded displayed in a public hall, including the chief mate who endures repeated near-death experiences with characteristic profanity.

The final movement describes the narrator's return to the river after twenty-one years' absence, traveling incognito. The landscape has transformed: steamboats are few, the levee is nearly empty, railroads and bridges have displaced river commerce. Uncle Mumford, a weathered mate, provides running commentary on river towns, changes in navigation, and the River Commission's attempts to tame the Mississippi. The narrator's incognito is detected by a pilot named Robert Styles, who loads him with elaborate lies about alligators until revealing his identity.

**I. Scene by Scene**

The text does not present a continuous narrative but unfolds as a series of argumentative movements, each building toward a cumulative critique of pagan religious practice and Roman historical self-justification.

The opening movement (Book 2, Chapter 26) pivots from a general accusation to a specific attack on pagan ritual practice. Augustine describes witnessing, or reports witnessing, obscene rites at the shrine of Cœlestis where "a grand display of harlots" stood beside "the virgin goddess." The juxtaposition reveals what Augustine presents as the fundamental contradiction at the heart of Roman religion: public rites that celebrate moral corruption, accompanied by private whispers of virtue offered only to initiates. This scene establishes the pattern Augustine will repeat throughout—the gods demand obscenity in public while reserving moral instruction for the few.

Chapter 27 turns to Cicero as authority, citing his advocacy for propitiating Flora through lewd games. Augustine reads the ten days of games during crisis not as devotion but as corruption invited under divine sanction: "to pacify them by debauchery." The scene here is argumentative rather than dramatic, built on textual citation, but it establishes the Romans' own acknowledgment that their religious practice was "wanton, impure, immodest."

Chapter 28 presents the contrast directly: the Christian church as sanctuary where "a seemly separation of the sexes is observed," where Scripture is proclaimed "from a raised platform in presence of all." This constitutes the positive pole of Augustine's argument—a vision of religious community structured by modesty rather than obscenity.

Chapter 29 issues an "exhortation to the Romans" that constitutes the climax of Book 2. Augustine addresses the Roman people directly, invoking their ancestral heroes (Scævola, Scipio, Regulus, Fabricius) as evidence that true virtue requires "true piety." He offers the church as "the celestial country" and frames the choice as liberation: "bursting forth into true liberty."

Book 3 begins with a methodological statement: Augustine announces he will now address "external and bodily disasters" rather than moral ones. This shift signals a double purpose—to show that Rome suffered without divine protection even in purely material terms, and to preempt the objection that Christianity receives blame for physical calamities.

Chapters 2-6 constitute a sustained examination of Troy's fall and Rome's origins. Augustine interrogates the mythology: if Laomedon's perjury angered the gods, why did Apollo and Neptune build Troy's walls despite anticipating betrayal? If Paris's adultery provoked punishment, why did Rome's founders commit comparable sins (the alleged fratricide of Romulus, the adultery attributed to Mars) without similar consequence? The argument proceeds through sequential refutation of apologetic positions.

Chapters 7-9 address Troy's later destruction by Fimbria and the period of Numa's peace. Augustine asks why Troy was abandoned a second time when it allied with Rome rather than opposed it. He questions whether Numa's peace really derived from the gods, or from favorable circumstances of his neighbors' behavior.

The text divides into distinct narrative movements, each serving different purposes in establishing the historical and biographical context for Marco Polo's travels.

The volume opens with an extensive system of notes and annotations spanning chapters II through LVII. The Admiral whispers urgently about a letter he has left for Lady Arpington, a letter entrusted to him by Admiral Kirby before his death, and asks Gower Woodseer to deliver it. Gower consents; the Admiral dies. The narrator reveals that the letter concerns the Countess Fanny Kirby's marriage to Captain John Peter Kirby—the secret union that produced Carinthia and Chillon—and that Admiral Kirby had wanted Lord Fleetwood to learn of it. The scene shifts to Gower in London, at his father's modest house among the Whitechapel poor. His father is a dissenting minister whose simple faith and relentless charity have earned him the nickname "the Welsh missionary." Gower watches him go out to visit the sick and distribute aid, noting the old man's inexhaustible good humor despite the misery he witnesses. His father moves among the suffering as though the dirt and desperation were nothing; he lifts his hat to them, speaks cheerfully, and refuses to be discouraged. Gower contrasts himself unfavorably with this serene acceptance: he is sickened by the poverty, haunted by the foreign woman's influence over him, and conscious that his own philosophy—whatever truth it contains—has failed to produce the equanimity his father displays without effort. His father's faith is "Nature at peace," while Gower's mind is "a workshop of machinery grinding against itself."

She is dressed simply, almost shabbily, but her bearing marks her as different. Gower observes her with the complicated admiration of a man drawn in two directions: he is drawn to her directness and her fearless engagement with the suffering, but he is also aware that she represents everything that has ensnared him—her beauty, her power over Lord Fleetwood, her foreignness. Plutarch introduces examples of Plato's imitators catching his stoop, Aristotle's his lisp, Alexander's his head tilt—vice spreading through intimacy like contagion. Plutarch distinguishes between praise bestowed on actions versus on persons, arguing that self-examination reveals whether praise is deserved: "if we are conscious, in the matters for which we get the praise, that we have not regretted them, and are not ashamed at them." He traces how flattery perverts language, calling wastefulness "liberality," cowardice "prudence," madness "quick-wittedness."

Sections XIII-XV detail flatterers' tactics: reporting others' panegyrics, fabricating charges to contradict, giving up seats

## Close Reading of "The Autobiography of a Yogi" (Chapters 30–37)

---

### 1. What Happens, Scene by Scene

The text opens in **Chapter 30** with an extensive philosophical meditation on light as the fundamental substance of creation. The narrator presents a 1937 New York Times report on the electron microscope's visualization of tungsten atoms, which he interprets as proof of "the light-essence of atoms" and the "duality of nature." He connects quantum discoveries—de Broglie's wave-particle duality, Davisson's Nobel-winning work—to ancient Vedic understanding. The chapter develops the "law of miracles": masters who can dematerialize and travel at light-speed have achieved infinite mass, fulfilling Einstein's condition that only infinite mass can equal light's velocity. The narrator then describes a personal vision in 1915, during World War I, where consciousness shifts between a battle scene (as a ship captain) and his body in Benares. A divine voice explains that "life or death" are irrelevant to Light, that creation is "a vast motion picture." A subsequent vision shows his body dissolving into light atoms projected onto his bedsheets, revealing cosmic reality as light-phenomena.

**Chapter 31** presents an interview with **Kashi Moni**, the wife of Lahiri Mahasaya, conducted by the narrator in Benares. She recounts a pivotal night when she witnessed her husband levitating among angels who were worshipping him. Recognizing his divine stature, she renounced him as husband and accepted him as guru, receiving Kriya Yoga initiation. She confesses a later moment of domestic resentment when she scolded him for neglecting family duties; he vanished, then materialized at the ceiling, scolding her for seeking material wealth. Additional anecdotes include a woman disciple (Abhoya) whose train stopped miraculously so she could reach Lahiri Mahasaya, and whose ninth child survived only through the master's intervention—appearing physically to relight a dying oil lamp. Another disciple, Kali Kumar Roy, describes how Lahiri Mahasaya materializes a vision of a woman to rebuke an skeptical employer. The chapter also introduces **Swami Trailanga**, a reputed 300-year-old nude yogi famous for surviving poisons, floating on the Ganges, and escaping jail.

**Chapter 32** recounts the resurrection of **Rama**, Sri Yukteswar's close friend. Rama, shy and reclusive, visited Lahiri Mahasaya only at midnight. He contracted cholera; despite the master's assurances that "Rama will be well," he died. Sri Yukteswar, in anguish, returned to the guru, who remained in samadhi. At dawn, Lahiri Mahasaya instructed Sri Yukteswar to administer seven drops of castor oil from a lamp to Rama's corpse. Upon the seventh drop, Rama revived, reporting he had seen the master "in a blaze of light" commanding him to arise. The guru later explains that his statements about the doctors had no causal connection with his prediction of Rama's wellness; divine healing operates independently of material circumstances.

**Chapter 33** introduces **Babaji** as the "Yogi-Christ of modern India," an avatara who has retained his physical form for centuries, perhaps millennia. The chapter explains the Sanskrit term *avatara* ("descent") and distinguishes Babaji as a *Mahavatar* whose mission involves assisting prophets and planning spiritual techniques for the age. Babaji's physical appearance is described: fair

## 1. What Happens, Scene by Scene

The text opens with **Norna's confession** to Minna and Brenda Troil. Norna responded defiantly, then fled. She later fell in love with a "stranger" against her father Erland's wishes, and when discovered, was confined to Hoy. She met her lover secretly to plan elopement, but inadvertently killed her father by closing his door (which trapped him with suffocating vapor). The conversation shifts to romantic attachments: Minna admits her love for Captain Cleveland, a mysterious sea captain staying at their home, while Brenda defends Mordaunt Mertoun, a young friend now fallen from favor. The sisters quarrel, reconcile, and agree not to tell their father about Norna's visit.

**The fate-telling oracle** takes place at breakfast. Magnus Troil, their father, hosts numerous guests. Instead of the housekeeper, Norna suddenly appears and takes the seat of the voluspa (prophetess). The company hesitantly consults her. Magnus asks about his whale-fishing; she predicts success. Halcro asks about his poetry; she responds obliquely. When Magnus asks about Brenda's marriage prospects, Norna gives a positive answer. But when he asks about **Minna**, the prophecy turns ominous—predicting "passion" that will "soil the wreath" and lead Minna to destruction. Magnus is angry, and when he calls Norna forth, she has vanished mysteriously.

**Cleveland and Minna's intimate conversation** occurs at the Helyer, a sea-cave. Cleveland confesses he cannot be friends with Mordaunt Mertoun due to "instinctive aversion." Minna encourages him to assert independence for Zetland. He declares his love, and Minna promises to bind herself to him by the "Promise of Odin"—a sacred Norse vow—until he returns. When Minna asks about his past, he tells of being marooned on Coffin-Key, where he forged his "iron mask" of ferocity to command his men. He admits he is a pirate, not merely a privateer. Minna is horrified that his comrades are "fiends," not noble Sea-Kings. She departs, telling him she must reflect.

**The departure and nocturnal sounds**: At breakfast, Cleveland announces he must sail immediately to Kirkwall on Bryce Snailsfoot's vessel. Mordaunt also departs coldly. That night, Minna cannot sleep. She hears Cleveland singing beneath her window—a Spanish love song. She tries to rise to speak with him but cannot wake Brenda, who sleeps in her arms.
