# Close Reading of the Opening Chapters of *The True History of the Conquest of New Spain*

---

## 1. What Happens, Scene by Scene

The text divides into two distinct movements. The first, covering roughly the opening pages, narrates the aftermath of Juan de Grijalva's expedition of 1518—the return to Cuba, the accounting of gold, Diego Velázquez's political machinations in Spain, and the fitting-out of a larger armada. The second movement, beginning with Chapter XIX, constitutes the actual departure of Hernando Cortés from Santiago de Cuba in February 1519.

**Scene 1 (pp. 1–6): Return and Accounting.** The narrator and his companions arrive back in Cuba from the Grijalva expedition. Diego Velázquez receives them gladly because of the gold—approximately 4,000 pesos added to the 16,000 brought by Alvarado, totaling 20,000. The crown's officials take only the fifths of the latter sum. The text notes embarrassment over Indian copper axes mistaken for gold. Velázquez is satisfied; his relative Grijalva is not, due to the intrigues of Alonso de Ávila, who is backed by Montejo. Rumor holds this dissension serves to prepare a new armament with a new commander.

**Scene 2: Velázquez's Chaplain Deputation (Chapter XVII).** Velázquez, fearing that court informants might steal his credit for the discovery, sends his chaplain Benito Martínez to Spain with letters and gold trinkets for Don Juan Rodríguez Fonseca (Bishop of Burgos), Louis Zapata, and Lope Conchillos. The narrator explains that Velázquez had gifted these patrons Indian villages in Cuba. Martínez obtains for Velázquez the title of Adelantado of Cuba, though this commission arrives only after Cortés has already departed.

**Scene 3: Critique of Gomara (Chapters XVIII–XIX opening).** The narrator interrupts his account to denounce Francisco López de Gomara's *History of the Conquest of New Spain*, which he discovered while writing his own. He catalogs Gomara's errors: inflated numbers of towns and inhabitants, misplaced commanders (e.g., Juan de Escalante confused with Pedro d'Irico at one battle), false claims about Cortés ordering the destruction of the eleven vessels (done unanimously), and silence on Hernández de Córdoba's prior discovery of Yucatán. The narrator accuses Gomara of distorting everything to Cortés's glory, omitting other brave officers, and dedicating his work to Cortés's son rather than the king. He vows to write a faithful account as an eyewitness.

**Scene 4: Selection of Cortés (Chapter XIX).** After Grijalva's return, Velázquez orders ten vessels fitted out at Santiago de Cuba. Various candidates for command are considered: Vasco Porcallo (deemed too daring and potentially independent), Agustín Bermúdez, Antonio Velázquez Borrego, Bernardino Velázquez (all relatives). The soldiers prefer Grijalva. Secretly, however, Velázquez's secretary Andrés de Duero and the royal treasurer Almador de Lares arrange the command for Hernando Cortés, who promises to share equally with them the profits from gold, silver, and jewels. Cortés is described as a cavallero of Medellín, son of Martín Cortés de Monroy and Catalina Pizarro Altamirano, recently married to Doña Catalina Suárez Pacheco. The narrator notes the marriage was expensive and caused Cortés's imprisonment. Duero and Lares lobby Velázquez successfully, praising Cortés's courage and noting that Velázquez had stood as witness at his wedding, creating a spiritual bond. Cortés is appointed captain-general.

**Scene 5: The Fool's Prophecy (Chapter XIX, end).** As Velázquez walks to church on the Sunday after the appointment, he honors Cortés by placing him on his right. A jester called "the fool Servantes" mocks the choice: "Well-a-day, friend Diego, what manner of a captain-general have you appointed? He of Medellín and Estremadura! A captain who wants to try his fortune in no small way. I am afraid he will cut his sticks with your whole squadron; for he is a terrible fellow when he once begins." Duero strikes the jester, calling him a drunken fool. The narrator notes that nobody doubted it was Velázquez's relative who had paid the fool to utter these complaints, and that everything the fool predicted later came true. The narrator comments: "It is nevertheless certain that the appointment of Hernando Cortés was pleasing in the eyes of God, a blessing to our holy religion, and of the first importance to his majesty."

The text opens in Rio de Janeiro with the narrator and Mac awaiting companions who have not arrived. The narrator arranges for Mac's concealment and luggage transfer to the steamer *Ebro*. The three conspirators spend an agonizing day waiting for the *Ebro* to sail, during which police chief and bank manager Braga search the vessel. Mac slips aboard undetected. The group then flees south through Montevideo and Buenos Aires to Marseille, regrouping in Paris.

His partners manufacture forged bills, leaving blanks for dates until ready for use. # Close Reading: The Vicomte de Bragelonne (Opening)

## 1. Scene by Scene

The passage divides into three parallel narrative threads, all set in 1643, shortly after the death of Louis XIII.

**Thread One: The Prison (Vincennes)**

The Duc de Beaufort, grandson of Henry IV. and popular with the Paris populace (the "king of the marketplaces"), has been imprisoned at Vincennes for five years under Governor de Chavigny, who petty torments him—replacing steel knives with silver ones, planting trees for shade, promising asparagus that will take four years to grow. Beaufort's frustration culminates in a speech to his keepers urging them to help him escape and "strangle Mazarin," but they refuse. Grimaud, an old servant of Athos sent by the conspirators, replaces La Ramee as the duke's keeper. Grimaud pretends to be hostile, confiscating the duke's leaden comb and glass shard, while secretly passing messages via tennis balls and a letter hidden in a ball from Rochefort (imprisoned in the Bastile but secretly outside). The escape is arranged: a special pâté from the new confectioner (Noirmont, the duke's former maître d'hôtel) will contain two poniards, a rope ladder, and a gag ("poire d'angoisse"). At Pentecost, La Ramee—whose weakness is gluttony—is plied with excellent food and wine. Beaufort narrates his escape plan aloud to distract La Ramee, then reveals the hidden weapons. La Ramee, rather than resist, asks to be bound and gagged so he won't be considered an accomplice. Beaufort and Grimaud descend via rope, Grimaud falling and injuring himself. They are met by Rochefort and two other gentlemen with horses. Beaufort escapes, shouting "Free! free! free!"

**Thread Two: Paris (The Introduction of Raoul)**

Athos (now the Comte de la Fère) and his ward, the Vicomte de Bragelonne (Raoul), arrive in Paris. Athos presents Raoul to the Duchess de Chevreuse, revealing that Raoul is the son of Marie Michon (Aramis's cousin), whom Athos met in 1633 during her flight to Spain. The child was born of that encounter; Athos has raised him secretly. The duchess, delighted, promises to help Raoul's career. Athos instructs Raoul to seek military service under the Prince de Marsillac, who will recommend him to Madame de Longueville, whose brother (the Prince de Condé) can give him a position. Raoul meets the young Françoise d'Aubigné (the future Madame de Maintenon) at the Abbé Scarron's salon. Scarron, the "queen's invalid" with a satirical wit, has just had his pension stopped by Mazarin; his rooms are the center of literary and political gossip. The coadjutor (Gondi, future Cardinal de Retz) is present, as is Aramis (now the Abbé d'Herblay). A secret meeting is arranged: tomorrow at six o'clock, at Saint-Mandé. Athos gives Raoul his father's sword and bids him farewell at Saint-Denis, instructing him to serve royalty, not merely the king. Raoul departs for the army.

He notes that Hooker ("our best British botanist and perhaps the best in the world") has become "a full convert" and that Huxley "is changed, and believes in mutation of species." The tone is one of cautious optimism amid anticipated controversy.

Shortly after publication, Darwin writes to Lyell (June 1859) thanking him for his volcanic work on Etna, revealing Darwin's ongoing engagement with geological questions while his species work circulates. By December 1859, Darwin reports to W.H. The correspondence documents the fierce debates that erupted in 1860. Sedgwick writes a hostile letter that Darwin describes as "terribly muddled, and really the first page seems almost childish." The quotation is "garbled," facts are misrepresented, and Darwin declares himself "heartily sorry that in your unselfish endeavours to spread what you believe to be truth, you should have incurred so brutal an attack."

# A Close Reading of the Introductory Pages to *The Book of Ser Marco Polo*

## 1. What Happens, Scene by Scene

The text you have provided does not narrate Marco Polo's travels themselves, but rather serves as an exhaustive scholarly introduction to those travels, tracing the Polos' biography from their departure from Venice in the thirteenth century through Marco's death and its aftermath. The progression moves through distinct episodes:

**The Return to Venice (Section 18):** Nicolò and Maffeo Polo arrive at Acre in April 1269, only to find that Pope Clement IV has died and no successor has been elected. They return to Venice, where Nicolò discovers his son Marco has grown into a fine fifteen-year-old lad, his wife having died during their absence. This scene establishes the family dynamics that will persist throughout—the brothers' long absences, the father finally meeting his grown son, and the textual dispute about whether Marco was born before or after Nicolò's departure (the "Pipino interpolation" that claims Marco was unborn when his father left).

**The Second Journey East (Section 19):** After two years of papal interregnum, the brothers cannot bear to disappoint the Great Kaan or abandon the "virgin field of speculation" they have discovered. They depart again, taking young Mark with them. At Acre, they consult Tedaldo Visconti, Archdeacon of Liège, for credentials. News arrives that Visconti has been elected Pope (Gregory X), and they return to Acre to finally execute the Kaan's commission—securing teachers and religious authorities. The new Pope provides only two Dominicans, who lose heart early. The passage opens with D'Artagnan and Porthos at an inn, where D'Artagnan recounts his recent interview with Cardinal Richelieu (a temporal displacement—the novel is set during the Fronde, but the Cardinal mentioned is clearly Richelieu, who died in 1642). The conversation concerns compensation for horses killed in service and the fate of a "parliament councillor" D'Artagnan crushed—a man who turns out to be Broussel, a popular Frondeur leader. The two friends divide the cardinal's payment and prepare to meet Athos and Aramis.

At the Place Royale, a site charged with political and personal memory, the four former musketeers confront each other. D'Artagnan accuses Athos and Aramis of deception at their respective castles—Athos at Bragelonne, Aramis at his convent—where they played games rather than answering his proposals. Aramis defends himself by noting that he gave D'Artagnan to understand he adhered to the princes, not Mazarin. The tension escalates until D'Artagnan rises and calls Aramis's conduct "worthy of a pupil of Jesuits." Athos, the moral center, breaks his sword rather than allow bloodshed, and his long speech invokes their shared past—"We lived together, we loved, we hated together; we shed, we mingled our blood together"—insisting that political divergence need not destroy personal bonds. They swear unity on Aramis's diamond cross, though D'Artagnan whispers to Aramis that they have sworn on the crucifix of a Frondeuse.

Raoul de Bragelonne, Athos's ward, rides toward the army of Prince Condé. He writes a letter to Athos full of longing and anxiety. He encounters the young Count de Guiche, son of Marshal de Grammont, at a ferry crossing where the rope snaps; Raoul swims to rescue Guiche, who cannot swim. They become fast friends and travel together. Near Arras, they encounter a Spanish ambush. During the skirmish, Raoul is wounded in the arm, Guiche shoots one Spaniard, and they capture a prisoner. They also find two travelers attacked: a dead priest and a wounded man who turns out to be the former executioner of Bethune, now serving as a curate's protector. The dying man demands a priest.

Raoul and Guiche find a monk traveling on a mule. The monk is young, pale, and unsettling. Despite his coldness, they compel him to accompany them. Back at the inn, the host recognizes the wounded man as "the former executioner of Bethune," and the monk's face shows "repugnance." Inside the room, the executioner confesses to the monk. He reveals that he once killed a woman at the orders of masked noblemen—this was Milady, whose real name was Anne de Bueil. He tells how she seduced his brother, a priest, and caused his death. The monk, increasingly agitated, demands the woman's name and learns it was indeed Anne de Bueil. The monk then announces: "I am John Francis de Winter" and reveals Milady was his mother. He stabs the executioner to death with a dagger, crying "Here is my absolution!" and escapes through the window.

Grimaud arrives at the inn and learns of the murder. The dying executioner tells him the monk "spoke no name" but knows "his uncle was among her judges"—that is, De Winter's brother, who was one of the four musketeers. ## 1. Scene-by-Scene Summary

The narrative opens with Marian learning from the housekeeper that Mrs. Catherick visited Blackwater Park while the household was away, an event Mrs. Catherick wished kept secret from Sir Percival. Marian notes the strangeness of this request given Sir Percival's claimed close relationship with Mrs. Catherick.

The travellers return: Sir Percival, Laura, and their guests, Count and Countess Fosco. Marian immediately observes changes in everyone—Sir Percival is thinner, more restless, more abrupt; Laura is physically altered (more colour, more decision) but spiritually diminished; and the Foscoes present alarming transformations. The Countess has become glacially silent and subdued, while the Count displays an uncanny mastery over everyone around him, including Marian's own reluctant attraction to him.

Mr. Merriman, Sir Percival's solicitor, arrives unexpectedly from London. Marian overhears him telling Sir Percival that "it all rests with Lady Glyde"—she must sign her name in presence of witnesses to seal some arrangement, otherwise bills at three months will be accepted. The conversation confirms Marian's fears: Sir Percival is in serious financial difficulty, and Laura is the key to his relief.

The next day, Sir Percival demands Laura sign a parchment document without explanation. Laura refuses until she knows what she is signing. Sir Percival erupts in abusive language, telling Laura she "made a virtue of necessity" by marrying him. Laura throws down the pen and turns her back on him in contempt. Count

## 1. What Happens, Scene by Scene

**Introductory Material (Chapter I-III):** The narrative opens with an embedded story about Charles Dump, a postillion who served the Squire Curtis. Dump, terrified of Squire Curtis, developed a habit of lying and ultimately died in ruin. Dr. Cawthorne, a noted botanist and turf man, inherited a portrait of Dump that hung in his reception room alongside a landscape painting of the Punch-Bowl. This establishes the text's preoccupation with storytelling, oral tradition, and the transmission of local legends.

**Chapter III:** Dame Gossip, the narrator, explains she has been entrusted with letters and documents from an old story. She describes the portrait of Charles Dump in detail: a small man diminished by wrinkles, with an enormous gay hat, sad countenance, and forefinger extended like a semaphore. Dump left a daughter, Mary Dump, who became lady's maid to Livia Fakenham, daughter of Curtis Fakenham. The narrative connects this humble origin to the aristocratic Fakenham family, noting that Livia later became Countess of Fleetwood, then widow, then married the Earl again.

**Chapter III (Continued):** The story shifts to Captain Kirby (the "Old Buccaneer") and Countess Fanny, who fled abroad. After the death of the Earl of Cressett, Kirby married Fanny in Switzerland. They had two children: Chillon Switzer John Kirby (born near Chillon Castle) and Carinthia Jane Kirby. Countess Fanny proved a virtuous wife despite foreign officers' immorality. Kirby worked a mine in Carinthia. Their son Chillon was educated in England but challenged a bully who slandered his mother. When Lord Levellier (the maternal uncle) intervened, Chillon was sent home wounded in spirit. Fanny told him her life story to protect him from future challenges to her reputation.

**Chapter III (Further):** Chillon secretly enlisted in Austrian Hussars but was recalled by Lord Levellier to a cornetcy in British dragoons. Countess Fanny advocated for England despite knowing it meant potential alienation. After her death (Chillon had been away), Kirby refused food and died in the mountain forest, his body discovered by Carinthia, her dog, and a servant.

**Chapter IV:** Chillon and Carinthia prepare to leave their mountain home for England. They spend a sleepless night, watch the dawn from the windows, and engage in their old game of "calling the morning" on a nearby hill. They descend through their estate—garden, brook, meadow, firwood—observing nature and remembering their father. At a cascade, Carinthia declares she will return to live and die there when she marries. The siblings argue briefly about walking versus driving to the Baths; Carinthia convinces Chillon to walk. They share a final meal at home with their old servant Mariandl, who has hidden provisions. Mariandl gives Carinthia tea tucked in her slipper and promises to place wreaths on their parents' grave. Chillon overrules Carinthia's acceptance of Count Lebern's hospitality; she must come to England under Lord Levellier's guardianship.

**Chapter V:** Mist rises as they walk. Carinthia asks about English ladies—specifically Livia (a young widow) and Henrietta Fakenham. Chillon shows her a portrait case with Henrietta's picture; Carinthia understands he loves Henrietta. They reach a village where Chillon arranges a car for the remainder of the journey. # Close Reading of *Ferdinand Count Fathom* (Chapters III–XVII)

## 1. What Happens, Scene by Scene

**Chapter III** introduces Ferdinand Fathom at age six, accompanying his mother—described as an "English Amazon"—into the military camp of Prince Eugene's imperial forces during the Ottoman-Austrian wars. She is a camp-follower who plunders the wounded and dying. She discovers and saves Colonel (later Count) Melvil, a Scottish officer, from the battlefield, and he reciprocates by taking Ferdinand into his protection and assuming responsibility for his education. Ferdinand's stepfather (the German) is killed in the trenches before Temiswaer, leaving Ferdinand entirely dependent on Melvil.

**Chapter IV** narrates his mother's death. She accompanies the army to battle at Belgrade, performs heroic acts including killing a Turkish aga, and is ultimately shot dead by a wounded hussar she attempted to rob. Ferdinand, now nine, is already weaned from maternal affection and continues in Count Melvil's household, where he distinguishes himself by filial piety (secretly kissing Melvil's hand and praying for him) and by exposing two soldiers plotting to desert and rob the Count's tent. Melvil retires to Presburg after the peace of Passarowitz and presents Ferdinand to his wife, an Hungarian Countess.

**Chapter V** depicts Ferdinand's education alongside the young Count Renaldo at a public academy. Ferdinand proves academically dull but socially adept—his dancing, deportment, and card-playing excel. He exploits a school exercise incident: when the young Count's translation of Caesar is identical to Ferdinand's (because Ferdinand copied Renaldo's work), the schoolmaster accuses Renaldo of plagiarism. Ferdinand, summoned, pretends tears and exonerates Renaldo while leaving ambiguous impressions that he himself was the wronged party. The schoolmaster spreads this misrepresentation, and Count Melvil rebukes his son while urging him to treat Ferdinand generously. Renaldo responds with increased kindness.

**Chapter VI** shows Ferdinand at sixteen, cultivating the affections of Count Melvil's daughter, Mademoiselle de Melvil. He uses studied reserve, musical performances, and romantic airs to attract her while avoiding premature declarations that might offend her pride. He feigns illness and delirium, prompting family concern, but Mademoiselle's comportment remains serene rather than passionate.

**Chapter VII** introduces Teresa, Mademoiselle's maid, who is herself in love with Ferdinand. He reciprocates strategically, proposing they become partners in exploiting the household. They agree to a clandestine "marriage of conscience" (an oath before Heaven rather than the Church) to secure mutual loyalty. Teresa agrees to help Ferdinand pursue Mademoiselle.

**Chapter VIII–IX** detail their conspiracy. Teresa pretends jealousy and defames Ferdinand, then Mademoiselle defends him—becoming habituated to his praises. Meanwhile, they frame a chambermaid for stealing Mademoiselle's purse. Ferdinand engineers the discovery, and Teresa's protestations of loyalty are rewarded with Mademoiselle's trust.

**Chapter X** escalates the theft: diamond earrings vanish. The chambermaid (already convicted of the purse theft) is imprisoned again, though ultimately released. Suspicion falls on everyone, including the young Count. Count Melvil sends Renaldo to Vienna to finish his education, with Ferdinand assigned as his companion, preceptor, and moral guardian. Ferdinand coaches Teresa on continuing operations and departs with gifts from the household.

**Chapter XI** depicts their arrival in Vienna. Ferdinand enters an alliance with a Tyrolese gamester. He engineers a scene where the Tyrolese "restores" Renaldo's gambling losses to maintain Ferdinand's reputation as Renaldo's protector while the Tyrolese continues fleecing him. Ferdinand's attempts at courtly gallantry are hampered by his lack of noble birth.

**Chapter XII** finds Ferdinand lodging with a wealthy Jewish jeweler. He courts both the wife (his stepmother, as it were) and the daughter Wilhelmina, encouraging their mutual jealousy. **Section XVI.** The essay opens mid-argument. Plutarch has been speaking about boys and now shifts to youths — young men past childhood but still in the dangerous period of sexual prime. He condemns parents who closely supervise boys but then release their sons into total liberty at the very age when they most need restraint. He catalogues the vices of youth: gluttony, theft from fathers, gambling, revelling, drinking, seduction. He insists this period is "prodigal in pleasure, and frisky, and needs a bridle," and that parents who do not restrain it are "foolishly, if unawares, giving their youths license for vice." The remedy is constant vigilance through "precepts, by threats, by entreaties, by advice, by promises, by citing examples" — both of those ruined by pleasure and those who attained praise through self-control. The two pillars of virtue, he argues, are "hope of honour, and fear of punishment."

**Section XVII.** He turns to the danger of bad company. Boys who associate with villains will "catch some of their villany." He cites Pythagoras' enigmatical precepts — allegorical maxims he interprets as moral teachings: "Do not touch black tails" (do not associate with bad men); "Do not go beyond the balance" (maintain justice); "Do not sit on a measure" (do not be idle); "Do not give everyone your right hand" (do not be too ready to strike up a friendship); "Do not wear a tight ring" (let your life be free); "Do not poke the fire with a sword" (do not provoke the angry); "Do not eat the heart" (do not pine away with anxiety); "Abstain from beans" (do not meddle in state affairs); "Do not put your food in the chamber-pot" (do not throw pearls before swine). He digresses to denounce flatterers especially — a "race more pestilential" than any other, who encourage sons to defy their fathers, who say "Our life's but a span," who pimp and procure, who "show their teeth and grinning all over when their patrons laugh." The father must banish this race from his house.

**Section XVIII.** Addressed now to fathers directly. Parents must not be over-harsh. They should "often forgive their sons' offences, remembering that they themselves were once young." The doctor who sweetens bitter medicine is the model. Fathers must "temper the severity of their censure by mildness," sometimes relaxing the reins, sometimes tightening them. It is better for a father to be hot-tempered than sullen — to continue hostile looks like hating one's son. Some faults should be overlooked entirely: "to extend to them the weak sight and deafness of old age, so as seeing not to see, and hearing not to hear." The text divides roughly into two arcs: Mina Murray's journal entries from Whitby (August) and London (August–September), and Dr. Seward's parallel account from his asylum. **Mina departs for Buda-Pesth** (19 August) on receiving a letter from Jonathan Harker, who has been recovering from brain fever for six weeks. The two marry quickly at the hospital. Mrs. Westenra dies of shock. Lucy's memorandum ends mid-sentence: she is alone with her dead mother, the servants drugged, the wolf howling outside.

She tells him that he is not truly exiled from his country, for his true country is God, who never abandons his citizens. She promises lighter remedies first, to soften his hardened passions before applying stronger medicine.

**Metre VI** follows: a meditation on proper timing—do not sow seeds when Cancer makes the earth hot, do not seek violets when the north wind blows, do not press grapes before autumn. God assigns times to things; whoever departs from this order finds no happy issue. **Prose VI** begins Philosophy's diagnostic examination. She asks whether the prisoner believes the world is governed by chance or by reason. He affirms belief in divine governance. She then asks what he remembers: the end of things, what he is, who he is. Through these questions, she diagnoses his malady: he has forgotten himself, forgotten the ends of things, and thus judges that wicked men are powerful and happy. She declares she has found the entrance to his recovery.

He distinguishes between prose and poetry by proposing that a poem's immediate object is pleasure, not truth, and that it creates delight through a harmonious whole where each part supports the others. He identifies four marks of genius: the sweetness of versification, the choice of subjects remote from the poet's personal experience, imagery modified by passion or that reduces multitude to unity, and depth and energy of thought. He argues that these poems show Shakespeare's power to make readers see and hear everything without being told directly.

In Chapter XVI, Coleridge contrasts the poetry of the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries with that of his own age. He notes that modern poets emphasize new images and interesting incidents with specific, individual characters, but are careless in diction and metre. In contrast, earlier poets, especially Italian ones, focused on general imagery and the manner of treatment rather than novelty of subject. Brandon, as a lawyer, is being offered a judgeship, and Mauleverer advises him to accept it, suggesting Brandon might even attain the chief-justiceship. Brandon reveals his health is failing: "I shall die before I have gained half my objects, if I do not leave the labours which are literally tearing me to pieces." He accepts the judgeship but insists the chief-justice or chief-baron position must be his eventual reward. Mauleverer then proposes to marry Lucy Brandon, whose £60,000 fortune excites him: "I have not a shilling for my own pleasure, though I have—or alas! had—fifty thousand a year for that of my establishment!"

**Scene 2: Lucy's Debut in Bath Society**

Lucy, now launched into "the gay world," becomes the object of universal idolatry. Her simplicity enhances rather than diminishes her reputation. The squire (Lucy's father) accompanies her everywhere but retreats into corners, "one of those persons who sink into a corner the moment they enter a room." Mauleverer cultivates the squire's goodwill while carefully avoiding substantive conversation with him.

**Scene 3: The Bath Ball**

At a grand ball graced by royalty, Lucy dances with Captain Clifford, a handsome stranger of "uncommon height," who arrives with two companions of dubious reputation. Mauleverer arrives late and observes Lucy dancing with Clifford: "How cursedly pleased she looks!" He discovers Clifford is unknown to the Master of Ceremonies, having arrived that evening. Mauleverer's jealousy is sharp but concealed beneath polished manner.

**Scene 4: The Thieves' Gathering**

In a mean alehouse in a remote suburb, Clifford presides over a meeting of "tax-collectors" (thieves). His confederates include Long Ned Pepper, Augustus Tomlinson, Old Bags, Fighting Attie, and others. Clifford delivers a speech resigning his captaincy but is immediately re-elected. The company drinks, sings, and divides their spoils. Tomlinson reveals the plan: "trying a matrimonial speculation at Bath—for an heiress." Clifford confesses he first met Lucy at Dr. Slopperton's house months earlier and has loved her ever since, but feels his life makes him "contamination" to her innocence.

**Scene 5: Brandon's Departure**

Brandon leaves Bath, entrusting Lucy to Mauleverer's guidance: "whomsoever he warns you against, you may be sure is unworthy of your acquaintance." He gives Lucy diamonds and implores her to consult Mauleverer on any matter, despite privately despising Mauleverer's vanity.

Clifford and Lucy walk together; their hands meet over a dropped flower. That evening at the squire's house, Lucy and Clifford sit together as night falls. **Close Reading: The Opening Chapters of the Book**

---

**1. What Happens, Scene by Scene**

The text opens in the midst of a rehearsal for the musical comedy *The Girl Up-stairs*. Rose Dane, the protagonist, makes a catastrophic entrance by forgetting her cues during a scene with Sylvia and the sextette. Her colleague Quan has lost his place in the script, and Rose sits paralyzed through a five-second stage wait that feels eternal. The author, present in the hall, mocks her inability to speak. Galbraith, the director, eventually rescues her by reading her line himself.

After this nadir, Galbraith offers Rose practical advice about voice projection—"a question of thinking where you want it to go"—and validates her suggested changes to her character's dialogue. From this point, Rose's career ascends. She earns the "tolerant esteem" of principals and pleasant speech from the owners themselves.

The narrative introduces two leading women in stark contrast: Patricia Devereux, who plays the title role, is "cool, brusk, hard finished" and professional, arriving at rehearsal with her street clothes and wrist-bag, having memorized her part perfectly before anyone else; and Anabel Astor, the "mercenary seductress," who has risen from chorus ranks, works with boundless vitality, and takes an immediate liking to Rose, calling her "dearie."

The text opens with a long sequence of footnotes (282–350) that function less as annotations than as a parallel discourse—glosses on Arab customs, Persian lore, vocabulary, and literary history. The first narrative, **The Tale of the Three Apples**, begins with Caliph Harun al-Rashid commissioning his Wazir Ja'afar to walk the city and assess the conduct of governors. They encounter an impoverished fisherman reciting verses about the wretchedness of learned men who cannot feed themselves. The Caliph buys the fisherman's catch for two hundred dinars. In the chest they find a woman's dismembered body. The Caliph, horrified that murder has occurred under his reign, threatens Ja'afar: find the killer within three days or he and forty of his Barmecide kin will be hanged.

On the appointed day, Ja'afar cannot produce the murderer and the execution is about to proceed when a young man forces through the crowd and claims the killing. An old man immediately counters, claiming the guilt himself. Both insist. Ja'afar takes both before the Caliph. The young man is interrogated. He explains that the slain woman was his wife and cousin. She had craved an apple during illness. He travelled to Basra, bought three apples for three dinars, and returned. Later he saw a black slave playing with one of the apples—his wife's apple. Enraged by the implication of infidelity, he murdered her, dismembered her, and cast her into the Tigris. When his young son later explained that a slave had taken the apple from him, the father understood the slave's lie had caused the murder. The youth then discovers the slave was Ja'afar's own property. Ja'afar's youngest daughter had purchased the apple from this slave, Rayhan, for two dinars. The Caliph finds the chain of causation astonishing, laughs, and orders the story recorded.

Ja'afar then promises to tell an even stranger tale—**the History of the Wazir Nur al-Din Ali of Egypt and his brother Shams al-Din Mohammed**—on condition the Caliph pardon his slave.

The second narrative, **The Tale of Nur al-Din Ali and His Son Badr al-Din Hasan**, opens with a just Sultan of Egypt and his aged Wazir, who has two sons of surpassing beauty, Shams al-Din (the elder) and Nur al-Din Ali (the younger). The Wazir dies; the Sultan appoints both sons joint ministers. One evening they agree to marry two sisters and consummate on the same night. Shams al-Din then proposes a dower of three thousand dinars, three pleasure gardens, and three farms for his prospective daughter-in-law (Nur al-Din's future son). Nur al-Din refuses, declaring the male line superior, and a bitter quarrel erupts. Shams al-Din leaves for a journey with the Sultan; Nur al-Din, furious, packs gold, mounts his mare-mule, and departs without destination. He travels through Bilbays, Sa'adiyah, Jerusalem, and Aleppo, eventually arriving at Basra, where he is seen by the aged Wazir of that city from his palace window. The Basran Wazir adopts him, lodges him honourably, and eventually proposes a marriage to his own daughter. Nur al-Din consents. The marriage is celebrated. Meanwhile, Shams al-Din returns, finds his brother gone, searches for him, despairs, and himself marries a Cairene merchant's daughter.

Both brothers' wives conceive on the same night, and both give birth on the same day—Nur al-Din's wife bears a son, Badr al-Din Hasan, and Shams al-Din's wife bears a daughter. The son grows to extraordinary beauty, educated by a Fakih, beloved by all. When he is twenty, his father Nur al-Din falls ill and, before dying, dictates his entire life story to be sewn into Hasan's skullcap. He gives five behests: (1) avoid over-intimacy with anyone; (2) deal harshly with no one; (3) learn silence; (4) shun wine; (5) guard wealth. Coleridge divides this into (a) laborious minuteness in representing objects and positions, and (b) insertion of accidental circumstances to explain characters and actions. He quotes Davenant's prefatory letter to Hobbes on poetry versus history. He cites lines from "The Excursion" (pages 96-98) as examples of excessive descriptive detail where visual art would suffice. ## 1. What Happens, Scene by Scene

The excerpt divides into two distinct narrative arcs, linked by Thackeray's characteristic technique of contrasting social worlds.

**First Arc: Paul's Downward Path**

The text opens with an anonymous "new critic" writing for "The Asinaeum" (a satirical version of *The Athenaeum*), whose obscure style Thackeray mocks before revealing this writer to be Paul. Paul has entered into an agreement with the Scotsman MacGrawler, who is meant to share profits from Paul's literary labor but instead keeps three-quarters for himself, giving Paul only a quarter. When Paul discovers MacGrawler has actually negotiated a payment of ten shillings per article (double the five shillings Paul believes is the standard rate), Paul leaves MacGrawler's house in anger.

## 1. What Happens, Scene by Scene

The passage opens with Davies and Carruthers sailing the *Dulcibella* through a violent storm in the Frisian sandbanks. They struggle against heavy seas, nearly swamped, but Davies's skill keeps them afloat. The storm passes, and over the next ten days they methodically explore the estuaries—Elbe, Jade, Weser—mapping channels and studying the sandbanks, their routines defined by tides and weather. They suffer a frightening stranding on the Rute Flat during a gale, surviving a night pinned on a lee shore. They eventually reach Bensersiel, a tiny mainland port, where they are boarded by Customs officers and meet Commander von Brüning of the German gunboat *Blitz*. Von Brüning engages them in a long, searching conversation, during which Davies lies about his September voyage with Dollmann. Von Brüning warns Carruthers not to revisit the Dollmanns and to leave the region. The *Blitz* tows them out. On the passage to Norderney, they encounter Fräulein Dollmann in her dinghy; she comes aboard and is shaken when she sees a book bearing her father's English naval identity. She flees in panic and begs Carruthers to prevent Davies from calling on them. Returning to the *Dulcibella*, Davies discovers the book is a yachting guide written by Dollmann when he was a British naval officer, confirming his English past. They decide their only course is to confront Dollmann directly and extract his secrets. They reach Norderney harbour in fog, intending to intercept Dollmann on his return the next morning.

---

## 2. Characters: Who Acts and What Drives Them

**Davies** drives the expedition. His conviction that the Frisian shallows constitute a perfect arena for torpedo-craft in wartime is both patriotic mission and personal obsession. He is driven by an almost religious devotion to the sandbank channels—"He could *smell* sand where he could not see or touch it." Yet this certainty is complicated by his love for Fräulein Dollmann, which he has concealed from Carruthers until the crisis at Bensersiel. His moral struggle between love and duty structures the later chapters. He is reckless in his devotion to the quest and to the woman, willing to hazard everything on a direct confrontation.

**Carruthers**, the narrator, is the cooler head, the diplomat, the reader's surrogate. His initial skepticism about the quest gradually gives way to commitment, though he retains a worldly pragmatism that allows him to lie to von Brüning and manipulate Fräulein Dollmann without scruple. He is driven by curiosity, by loyalty to Davies, and by a growing sense that the work "meant something." His cynicism about the duck-shooting cover and his facility with German make him the essential complement to Davies's innocence.

**Commander von Brüning** is the most unsettling presence. A German naval officer, he is courteous, witty, and thoroughly hospitable—yet his questions are surgical. He knows more than he reveals and warns Carruthers away from the Dollmanns without explaining why.

## 1. Scene-by-Scene Summary

**1. What happens, scene by scene**

The text opens with a scene at an inn in Paris where a group of French gentlemen have been sent by a mysterious letter they interpret as either a challenge or an invitation to reconciliation. They find the writer—an abbé—dressed absurdly: three nightcaps, a crape bandage across his face. The abbé is surprised by their errand, then is delighted to learn they have come to apologise for an unintended offence. He claims his nose is injured (it is not), and the company condoling him leads into a domestic settlement of their quarrel. After this reconciliation the company, including the protagonist, attend a comedy and then go to a count’s lodgings to play quadrille. The protagonist wins twenty louis, suspects the others are concealing their skill, and guards against their future designs.

The next phase describes how the protagonist, now Ferdinand, avoids the advances of the three men—the count, the abbé, and their companion—whose coalition he perceives as a threat. He maintains his dignity and reserve, convinced they are feigning novitiate to strip him on some future occasion. At a Parisian ordinary, a startling figure arrives: an Englishman dressed exactly as a jockey, complete with leathern cap, fustian frock, flannel waistcoat, buff breeches, hunting-boots and whip. He cracks his whip like a cohorn and shouts foxhunter cries. The company mistakes him for a maniac. He turns out to be Sir Stentor Stile, an English baronet who has come to Paris on a wager: he will appear daily in public walks for a month in this dress, for a thousand pounds laid by Squire Snaffle. The other English knight present, Sir Giles Squirrel, greets him with exuberant embraces, to the amusement of the company. Sir Stentor is blunt, boastful, contemptuous of French food, and proud of English wealth and plainness. Ferdinand is thrilled to perceive him as a naïve and wealthy mark, and determines to supplant Sir Giles in his favour.

Ferdinand ingratiates himself with Sir Stentor, and they agree to drink together. At an auberge, Sir Stentor gets drunk, sings "The Early Horn" at the top of his voice, and grows affectionate. Sir Giles becomes so drunk he collapses and is put to bed. Ferdinand, still sober, claims to be the head of a noble Polish family, forced to leave Poland on account of an affair of honour. They swear eternal friendship. Sir Stentor proposes a game of chance; Ferdinand claims ignorance of lansquenet but suggests they play at hazard. Sir Stentor says he is no money-seeker, has a good estate of five thousand a year, and offers to toss up for a guinea or play dice. Ferdinand conceals his delight: hazard is his specialty, and he can calculate all chances. He lets Sir Stentor win twenty broad pieces, then turns the tables with his arithmetic. Sir Stentor loses, grows furious, stamps, curses his luck, accuses Ferdinand of using false dice, throws the dice out of the window, and threatens him before he leaves.

The stakes are raised repeatedly. By dawn Sir Stentor has won all Ferdinand's ready cash, jewels, and almost everything valuable about his person, and taunts him about receiving another remittance from Poland. The chapter ends with Ferdinand reflecting that he has been outwitted at his own game, robbed of his resources, and recognises that the dice were loaded against him. He resolves to accommodate his fate, learn the lesson, and press on.

Ferdinand dismisses his valet, quits his lodgings, and relocates across the Seine. He disguises himself as a one-eyed musician, presenting himself to the director of the opera under the name of Fadini. He is admitted to the band and over ten months lives frugally, saving a purse for future operations. He observes a tall, thin Persian man living in the same house, named Ali Beker. The Persian is melancholy, often sighs, and is watched by the police but found harmless. Ferdinand curries his acquaintance, eventually lending him a small sum that saves his life. Ali's reserve is overcome, and one night he reveals his true identity: he is Don Diego de Zelos, a Castilian nobleman. He recounts his military career, his bravery in battle, his rescue of Don Gonzales Orgullo, his marriage to Gonzales's daughter Antonia, and the birth of their daughter Sera
